title: Global Payments faces industry pricing pressure
snippet: While analysts point to an increasingly competitive environment for the processor, the company is still trying to raise prices.
fullText:
Global Payments and other processors face an increasingly competitive market, with rising pricing pressures forcing some businesses in the ecosystem to consider consolidation.

Global Payments has touted increased merchant acceptance of its Genius point-of-sale services brand, but now it may be trying to force through price hikes in an increasingly competitive market.

The payments processing company is seeking to implement a new $699 annual fee for its merchant clients next month, according to a merchant consultant who posted a portion of a Global Payments letter on LinkedIn. 

“Worldpay, now part of Global Payments, is introducing a $699 annual fee, with the first charge hitting merchant statements this December. Yes, another one,” Merchant Cost Consulting Partner Matt Rej said in the LinkedIn post last week. “And this is on top of the other increases we've already seen from Worldpay this year.”

Rej questioned, and poked fun at, the reasoning Global Payments provided for the increase, pointing to the company’s letter saying: “Government and industry regulations have had a significant impact on system requirements in the payment processing industry.”

The Atlanta-based company didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment. Nonetheless, in its third-quarter earnings press release last week, the company acknowledged “increased competition in the markets in which we operate.”

Global Payments pricing moves come less than a year after it completed its $24.25 billion purchase of the merchant services company Worldpay, which could give the company stronger pricing power in the industry. In the third-quarter report, Global Payments reported that the Genius brand, which was launched last year, was placed at 65% more merchant locations, compared to the year-earlier period, and bookings more than doubled.   

As the Genius brand gains traction, the company is reportedly considering selling itself off to one of its largest shareholders, private equity firm GTCR, and the investment firm Clayton, Dubilier & Rice. GTCR is acquainted with Global Payments partly because it was one of the companies that sold it the Worldpay assets.

Any fee increases by POS service providers are increasingly met with pressure from younger financial technology companies building a presence in the market with newer technologies. As a result, some legacy companies that provide payments services to merchants, including behemoth Fiserv, the new entrant Shift4 and the Dutch company Adyen, are feeling a competitive crunch.

Point-of-sale services firm PayCompass said in September that it had merged with two other firms and the CEO at the merchant services provider Butter Payments said last month that the company had sold its assets to an unnamed buyer.

While analysts who follow Global Payments praised the company’s progress in integrating Worldpay into its operations and luring merchants to the Genius brand, they noted the increasingly competitive market. As such, price increases may be a tough sell, particularly as merchants face consumers stretched by inflationary pressures. 

Analysts at the investment firm William Blair raised concerns about Global Payments technology being capable of competing with new fintechs.

“While sales metrics appear strong, we argue Genius is simply not a competitive offering from a technology standpoint and will not become material enough to durably accelerate consolidated organic growth,” the analysts said in a Thursday note to their clients, acknowledging the brand’s third-quarter growth.

Other analysts who follow the company also pointed out the competitive intensity in the market in commenting on Global Payments results.

“The Payments industry is very competitive with both existing and emerging competition,” analysts for TD Cowen told clients in a note Thursday. “All of our companies face the risk of being unable to capture market share or having their business models become commoditized by newer entrants in the market. Additionally, our companies are levered to consumer spending and therefore are exposed to general economic conditions.”

Analysts who follow the company for the investment firm R.W. Baird called out the difficulties for raising prices at this time across the industry. “Pricing pressure is a constant threat, and new fintechs have become competitive threats as well,” analysts at the Baird Equity Research arm said in a Thursday note. 

A sale to private owners might relieve some of the pressure of operating in the publicly traded market, with its focus on quarterly reports. Still, the analysts at William Blair last week gave the deal less than a 50-50 chance of being completed, partly because of the debt that Global Payments has in the wake of its Worldpay deal.

In a prior Oct. 30 note focused exclusively on the reports of a potential Global Payments sale, the William Blair analysts said that some $22 billion of debt at the company “could be an impediment, especially in a rising rate environment.”

The William Blair analysts posited that they could be wrong about the chances of the sale. If they are, they forecast that other “debt-laden” publicly traded companies in the industry, including Shift4 Payments and Fiserv, “pressure to sell will ratchet up dramatically, setting up what could be the final wave of industry consolidation.”

FCA to explore quantum computing to tackle financial crime

              

  

  

  
    

        

    

      

A new initiative will bring together firms, quantum technology providers, and national research labs to explore practical applications of quantum computing.

  

            						

The FCA will bring together financial services firms, quantum technology providers and national research laboratories to explore how quantum computing could help tackle financial crime.

The Quantum Experimentation Group, the first of its kind for a regulator, will initially explore how quantum machine learning could help detect money laundering and fraud. It will launch in the first quarter of 2027.

Participants will use an FCA synthetic dataset – artificially generated data – to help overcome a key barrier to testing: access to suitable data.

The group will help firms explore practical uses of quantum computing in financial services and share findings to guide future testing. It will also help the FCA understand the technology’s opportunities and limitations, barriers to experimentation and what these could mean for regulation.

Jessica Rusu, chief data, information and intelligence officer at the FCA, said: 'We want to help firms explore where quantum could make a meaningful difference, and early experimentation is essential to understanding its potential in financial services. By bringing together firms, technology providers and researchers we can build readiness and identify practical applications for common industry challenges, starting with financial crime.'

The initiative builds on the FCA’s research into the long-term potential of quantum computing in financial services.

Financial services firms, quantum technology providers and national research laboratories can register their interest in joining the group by 31 December 2026.

Notes to editors

Read more about the Quantum Experimentation Group and how to register an interest in joining the group.

The FCA’s Quantum Experimentation Group will be the world’s first regulator-led quantum computing experimentation group.

The group will support organisations at different stages of their quantum journey, from those beginning to explore potential use cases to those already undertaking advanced experimentation.

As part of the initiative, the FCA will define problem statements and work alongside participants to build understanding of the opportunities, limitations and practical considerations associated with quantum technologies.

The initiative will complement wider activity across the UK’s quantum ecosystem by creating additional opportunities for collaborative experimentation and learning.

title: Vertice Launches Procure-to-Pay to Close Post-Contract Value Leak
snippet: The London AI procurement platform says its new P2P module targets the 10%-plus of contract value that leaks after signing through missed discounts and The post Vertice Launches Procure-to-Pay to Close Post-Contract Value Leak appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Vertice, the London-based AI procurement platform, has launched a Procure-to-Pay (P2P) capability that extends its existing Intake-to-Procure product into invoice processing, purchase-order matching, spend controls and supplier payments. The company says the move creates a single record spanning every stage from initial purchase request to final settlement, giving finance and accounts payable teams unified visibility over data that is typically scattered across multiple systems.

The launch targets a specific and quantifiable inefficiency. According to a January 2026 report by World Commerce and Contracting, companies on average lose more than 11% of contract value after the deal is signed, through missed early-payment discounts and payment terms that drift in favour of the supplier. Vertice claims that customers running suppliers through the new P2P module have already unlocked faster payment cycles, better terms or improved cost forecasts for more than 80% of those relationships.

What the platform does

Eldar Tuvey, co-founder and CEO at Vertice

The intelligence layer underpinning the P2P module is Vertice’s proprietary spend dataset, which the company describes as covering $75 billion of processed spend across 32,000 vendors. The dataset is used to contextualise each invoice and contract against live market pricing, helping finance teams assess whether the terms they negotiated remain competitive and where a supplier is likely to accept renegotiation. AI agents handle the operational layer: classifying invoices, extracting data, reconciling against purchase orders and contract terms, and appending general-ledger codes and audit trails.

Eldar Tuvey, chief executive and co-founder of Vertice, said the core problem is one of visibility. “Finance teams can’t protect value if all they can see is a PO and an invoice,” he said. “We are giving Finance the visibility, context and automation they need to easily plug these leaks.”

Patrick Reymann, research director for procurement applications and agents at IDC, said extending the dataset to the payment layer was a logical progression from Vertice’s existing positioning. IDC named Vertice a Leader in its 2026 MarketScape for worldwide AI-enabled spend orchestration.

Market context

The procure-to-pay software market is well-populated. Established enterprise resource planning vendors bundle P2P modules as part of broader finance suites, while dedicated procurement platforms including Coupa, Ivalua and Zip have competed on workflow automation and supplier network depth. The differentiator Vertice is staking is the proprietary benchmark dataset: the argument is that knowing what other buyers pay the same vendor is worth more than workflow automation alone, because it shifts the negotiating posture rather than merely streamlining the paperwork.

That claim is plausible but depends on dataset quality, coverage breadth and recency, none of which Vertice has opened to independent audit. The 80% supplier improvement figure is an early-customer metric rather than a controlled study, and the absence of a defined baseline makes it difficult to assess. Buyers evaluating the platform will want to understand the vendor coverage within their own spend categories before committing.

The commercial case is sharpened by the current macro environment. With borrowing costs still elevated relative to the pre-2022 cycle, treasury and procurement teams are under pressure to optimise working capital actively rather than passively. Early-payment discount capture and dynamic payment-term management are straightforward levers, and automating them at the invoice level removes the manual reconciliation overhead that typically prevents finance teams from acting on them at scale.

Named customers including ARM, Brex, Duolingo, Twilio and Santander lend credibility to the enterprise positioning. The Financial Times recognised Vertice as the UK’s fastest-growing scale-up, though the criteria and year of that designation were not specified in the release. Vertice operates across six offices including New York, Sydney and Johannesburg, and says its platform is used in more than 100 countries. Procure-to-Pay is available immediately as part of the core platform.

title: Mojo Mortgages: Income Caps will Block 13% from ‘Your First Home’
snippet: Data from Mojo Mortgages shows proposed household income limits will exclude over 13% of first-time buyer applicants nationally, rising to 22% in London. The post Mojo Mortgages: Income Caps will Block 13% from ‘Your First Home’ appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Andy Burnham‘s proposed ‘Your First Home’ scheme aims to cut the minimum deposit for first-time buyers to 2.5%, backed by a government equity loan covering 20% of the purchase price. New data from online mortgage broker Mojo Mortgages suggests the scheme’s income eligibility rules will bar a significant portion of the buyers it was designed to help.

John Fraser-Tucker, head of mortgages at Mojo Mortgages

According to Mojo’s internal customer data, the proposed household income caps of £90,000 outside London and £110,000 within Greater London would exclude more than 13% of first-time buyer applicants nationwide. In London and the surrounding area, that figure climbs to over 22%. The disproportionate impact on dual-earner couples in high-cost cities is the central tension the broker’s analysis highlights: two people each earning average London wages can easily clear the £110,000 threshold while still lacking sufficient savings to fund a conventional deposit.

John Fraser-Tucker, head of mortgages at Mojo Mortgages, said: “Lowering the deposit barrier to 2.5% addresses one of the single biggest hurdles first-time buyers face. However, introducing strict household income caps creates a delicate balancing act. Two average working earners buying together, especially in high-cost regions, can easily cross these thresholds, effectively locking out working couples who are already squeezed by high property values.”

The savings landscape behind the numbers

The same data set illustrates how first-time buyers are already adapting to structural affordability pressures. A Mojo Mortgages survey conducted by Censuswide in April 2026, covering 1,000 UK first-time buyers, found that 64% rely on side hustles such as resale platforms or freelance income to build their deposit savings, with 53% of that cohort reporting the additional income shortened their savings timeline by two to three years. A further 22% said they had remained in roles they described as toxic solely to maintain the income stability required for a mortgage application. Some 26% still relied on a gifted family deposit to complete a purchase.

Five schemes, five trade-offs

The release accompanies a full breakdown of the five current or proposed government-backed routes to homeownership. Beyond ‘Your First Home’, the active options include the Lifetime ISA, which offers a 25% government bonus on savings up to £4,000 per tax year but is capped at properties priced below £450,000; the First Homes Scheme, which provides a 30% to 50% discount on new-build properties for local key workers but suffers from severely constrained availability; the Mortgage Guarantee Scheme, which enables 95% LTV borrowing on open-market properties but at higher interest rates; and Shared Ownership, which calculates the deposit against a purchased share rather than full property value but layers in ongoing rent and service charges on top of mortgage payments.

Market context

The broader proptech and mortgage-fintech market has seen a wave of digital broker services competing on speed of comparison and the quality of eligibility tooling. Mojo, which compares products from more than 60 lenders, sits in a segment that includes Habito and Trussle. The commercial value of this kind of analysis is partly editorial, establishing the broker as the authoritative voice on scheme eligibility, and partly lead generation, the release closes with a prompt to consult a Mojo adviser.

The policy stakes are real, however. The interaction between income caps and property prices in London has been a recurring failure mode for previous help-to-buy iterations. Policymakers drafting the final ‘Your First Home’ legislation will need to determine whether the income thresholds should be indexed to regional property price-to-income ratios rather than set as fixed nominal figures. If they are not adjusted, the scheme risks replicating the geographic inequity of its predecessors even before a single mortgage is drawn down.

title: Standard Chartered Acquires Zodia Custody in Digital Assets Push
snippet: Standard Chartered has signed definitive agreements to buy 100% of Zodia Custody, consolidating its institutional digital asset custody operations globally. The post Standard Chartered Acquires Zodia Custody in Digital Assets Push appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Standard Chartered has entered into definitive agreements to acquire Zodia Custody, the institutional digital asset custodian it helped establish through its SC Ventures innovation arm. The transaction, announced on 21 October 2026, will see Standard Chartered I H Limited acquire 100% of Zodia Custody Limited, the parent of regulated operating entities spanning Singapore, Hong Kong, Australia, the United Arab Emirates and Luxembourg. Completion remains subject to regulatory approvals and customary closing conditions.

Once integrated, Zodia Custody’s regulated business will sit inside Standard Chartered’s Securities Services division alongside its existing digital asset custody activities in the UAE and Luxembourg. The bank says the combination is intended to create a unified offering that covers both traditional and digital asset securities for institutional clients, removing the operational separation that has existed between the two lines.

The carve-out: Zodia Solutions

Ying Ying Tan, global head of securities services and digital assets at Standard Chartered

A notable structural feature of the deal is the concurrent separation of Zodia Custody’s software and professional services arm. That business will be transferred to a newly established entity, Zodia Solutions, housed under SC Ventures rather than absorbed into the bank’s core. Zodia Solutions will continue to provide bank-grade custody infrastructure to financial institutions, including Standard Chartered itself.

A consortium of bank investors will support Zodia Solutions, including NAB Ventures, Northern Trust Corporation, SBI Ventures, Further Ventures (Q Studio), Emirates NBD, Investcorp’s Zodia Investments, and SC Ventures. The structure effectively preserves the vendor relationship with third-party institutions while giving Standard Chartered full ownership of the regulated custody entity. No financial terms for either the acquisition or the capitalisation of Zodia Solutions were disclosed.

Ying Ying Tan, global head of securities services and digital assets at Standard Chartered, said the deal “deepens our digital asset custody portfolio and reinforces our position as a leading provider of digital asset services globally, supported by the depth, breadth and global connectivity of an international cross-border bank.”

Market and regulatory context

Richard Clark, CEO at Zodia Custody

The acquisition reflects a broader consolidation trend in institutional digital asset custody. As regulators in major jurisdictions have moved to clarify the treatment of crypto assets held on behalf of clients, the custody layer has become a strategic priority for tier-one banks rather than a speculative adjacency. In the EU, MiCA’s requirements for crypto-asset service provider authorisation have accelerated demand for licensed custodians with established banking relationships. In Asia, Hong Kong’s VASP licensing regime and Singapore’s MAS framework have similarly pushed institutional clients towards regulated, bank-affiliated counterparties.

Standard Chartered’s move brings regulated custody licences across five jurisdictions into a single ownership structure, which is a meaningful regulatory footprint. Few custodians of any type can offer that breadth under one bank’s balance sheet, and the combination with an established securities services business creates a cross-sell opportunity into the bank’s existing institutional client base.

Competitors in the institutional custody space include Anchorage Digital, Copper and Coinbase Custody at the specialist end, as well as BNY Mellon and Citigroup, which have been building digital asset custody capabilities within their own securities services businesses. The Standard Chartered and Zodia Solutions model, where the software platform remains available to third-party banks, is an attempt to capture infrastructure revenue beyond the bank’s own custody clients.

Richard Clark, chief executive of Zodia Custody, noted that “custody is increasingly becoming part of the global banking landscape” as institutional adoption accelerates. The next markers to watch are which jurisdictions grant regulatory approval first and how quickly the combined custody offering is brought to market for Securities Services clients.

title: Western Union Scraps Intermex Deal After Regulatory Fight
snippet: Western Union has terminated its agreement to acquire International Money Express (Intermex) after reaching what it described as an impasse with California regulators. California’s Department of Financial Protection and Innovation (DFPI) announced Tuesday (Nov. 11) that it had given conditional approval to the deal, provided the companies comply with the regulator’s consumer protection concerns. Soon […] The post Western Union Scraps Intermex Deal After Regulatory Fight appeared first on PYMNTS.com.
fullText:
Western Union has terminated its agreement to acquire International Money Express (Intermex) after reaching what it described as an impasse with California regulators.

California’s Department of Financial Protection and Innovation (DFPI) announced Tuesday (Nov. 11) that it had given conditional approval to the deal, provided the companies comply with the regulator’s consumer protection concerns.

Soon after, Western Union issued a statement calling off the deal, arguing that the DFPI’s conditions would have “required material changes” to its business model, agent relationships and long-term business strategy. 

“Western Union viewed these conditions as substantial and not in the best interests of Western Union, its agents or its shareholders,” the statement said.

The DFPI said its conditions were designed to prevent fraud, scams and money laundering and ensure “fair and competitive access to financial services.”

Western Union noted that the regulator had not found any failures on the company’s part to comply with legal requirements for scam and fraud prevention, money laundering and providing consumers with “fair and competitive access.”

Western Union announced the planned $500 million deal last year, saying it would help strengthen its U.S. retail business and speed digital customer acquisition.

“Intermex has built a well-recognized brand, as well as strong agent and customer relationships,” Western Union President and CEO Devin McGranahan said in a new release at the time. “Together, we will expand our retail footprint, unlock operational efficiencies and accelerate digital engagement.”

The deal has faced pushback from other avenues. As covered here in May, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdami had asked the New York State Department of Financial Services (NYDFS) to block the deal, arguing it would put financial pressure on the city’s immigrants.

The NYDFS ultimately granted its approval in August after Western Union made certain commitments related to remittance services and locations in New York after the acquisition.

Around the same time, Western Union said the DFPI had suspended an approval extension it had granted to the pending acquisition, citing the need for further review.

As recently as last week, Western Union was still working on the deal, with McGranahan saying during an earnings call that the company had gotten feedback from the DFPI and was “actively working to determine an acceptable path forward.”

“November 10, 2026, is the outside date included in the merger agreement, at which point either party has a right to terminate the agreement,” the CEO added.

title: Aero Launches on Seven Chains as Aerodrome and Velodrome Merge
snippet: The combined DEX, built on Dromos Labs' MetaDEX03, targets $121bn in monthly trading volume across Ethereum, Base, Robinhood Chain and four other networks. The post Aero Launches on Seven Chains as Aerodrome and Velodrome Merge appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Aerodrome and Velodrome, the dominant decentralised exchanges on Base and OP Mainnet respectively, merged on 21 October 2026 to form Aero, a multi-chain spot exchange launching simultaneously across seven networks: Arbitrum, Arc, Base, Ethereum Mainnet, Ink, OP Mainnet and Robinhood Chain.

The combined entity is built on MetaDEX03, a new exchange operating system developed by Dromos Labs, Aero’s core contributor. No venture capital backing or token sale accompanies the launch. Existing AERO and VELO holders upgrade to the new AERO token, with veAERO and veVELO positions converting to sAERO. The token split reflects each predecessor’s revenue share over the 52 weeks prior to the merger announcement: 94.5% to the Aerodrome community and 5.5% to Velodrome.

What Aero brings together

The constituent protocols had individually established strong market positions before the merger. In Q3 2026, Aerodrome handled 58% of DEX volume on Base and Velodrome 60% on OP Mainnet, according to Blockworks data. Aerodrome also led all DEXs in bitcoin-dollar spot volume over the same period, with a 29% share, and accumulated $2.80 billion in onchain FX spot volume in the first half of 2026, ahead of all other DEXs combined. Its share of tokenised-stock trading on Ethereum and its layer-2 networks climbed from under 3% in early September to 57% on 10 October, a period in which Coinbase’s tokenised-equity product provided a distribution tailwind.

Together, the two protocols have distributed $578 million in lifetime exchange revenue to tokenholders, a figure the company says ranks first among all DEXs by that metric on DefiLlama’s holder-revenue rankings.

The seven launch chains handled approximately $121 billion in DEX volume in the 30 days to 14 October 2026, against $32 billion on Base and OP Mainnet alone, according to DefiLlama. Aero positions the merger as access to roughly four times its predecessors’ addressable volume.

The protocol’s headline product innovation is Predictive Allocation, a liquidity-incentive mechanism inspired by prediction markets. Staked AERO holders direct the exchange’s liquidity-rewards budget toward pools they expect to generate revenue, earning a proportional share of 100% of that revenue in real time. The company says this should attract liquidity ahead of demand rather than reactively, which it argues is a structural improvement over the industry norm. Supporting features include Metaswaps for single-transaction cross-chain execution, SlipstreamV3 with dynamic fees and MEV capture on supported layer-2 networks, and onchain data contracts designed to allow AI agents and aggregators to integrate directly without custom development.

Market context and regulatory read-across

Multi-chain DEX aggregation is an increasingly contested space. Uniswap already operates across multiple EVM-compatible networks and commands significant brand recognition among both retail and institutional traders. Curve Finance built its dominance on stablecoin and FX liquidity, the same segment where Aerodrome accumulated its H1 lead. The tokenised-equity vertical is newer and moves faster: the speed at which Aerodrome went from under 3% to 57% of that flow reflects how quickly market structure can shift when a well-capitalised distribution partner, in this case Coinbase, accelerates adoption.

On the regulatory side, tokenised stocks sit in an uncertain cross-jurisdictional frame. In the US, the SEC‘s posture toward tokenised securities remains unsettled, and the instruments Aerodrome has been trading are typically structured to avoid classification as registered securities. MiCA in the EU addresses crypto-asset service providers but does not yet fully resolve the treatment of tokenised equities. Any exchange moving into this asset class at scale will face increasing regulatory attention as volumes grow, particularly across jurisdictions with differing securities rules.

Smart-contract security is a credible concern at this scale. Aero’s contracts were audited by ChainSecurity, Blackthorn, Riley Holterhus and GregoAI, followed by a three-week public contest on Sherlock, with a bug bounty live at launch. The quality of that coverage will be tested under live trading conditions across seven networks.

Alex Cutler, chief executive and founder of Dromos Labs, said: “Every market is coming onchain, and any institution that can be distilled into code will be. Their margin is our opportunity.”

title: Exim Bank Uganda Launches TerraPay-Powered Cross-Porder Payment Service
snippet: Exim Global Pay connects Ugandan retail and business customers to TerraPay's network spanning 156 countries and 7.5 billion bank accounts. The post Exim Bank Uganda Launches TerraPay-Powered Cross-Porder Payment Service appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Exim Bank Uganda Limited has launched Exim Global Pay, a cross-border payment product built on TerraPay‘s global payments infrastructure. The service is designed to let individuals and businesses in Uganda send money internationally through their existing banking relationship, covering use cases from supplier payments to education fees and family remittances.

The bank said the product responds to what it describes as growing international payment needs among Ugandan consumers and businesses, as the country becomes more integrated into global trade and education flows. Exim Bank Uganda operates seven branches and more than 9,500 agents through a shared platform, giving the product a relatively broad domestic distribution base from day one.

TerraPay’s model centres on providing a single integration point through which partner banks and financial institutions can reach its network, rather than requiring each institution to build and maintain multiple bilateral correspondent relationships. The company says its infrastructure covers 156 countries, connects to more than 7.5 billion bank accounts and reaches mobile wallets and cards as well as traditional accounts.

The deal

Edward Kanyike, managing director at Exim Bank Uganda

Edward Kanyike, managing director of Exim Bank Uganda, said the launch reflects a wider shift in how customers expect international transactions to work. “A business in Kampala can transact with a supplier thousands of kilometres away, a parent can pay for a child’s education overseas, and an individual can have financial commitments in more than one country. What should not remain complicated is the payment that makes these transactions possible.”

Willie Kanyeki, vice president for Sub-Saharan Africa at TerraPay

Willie Kanyeki, TerraPay’s vice president for Sub-Saharan Africa, framed the partnership in infrastructure terms. “Cross-border payments should enable economic participation, not create friction around it,” he said. “It is another step towards building greater interoperability between local financial institutions and global payment networks.”

The release did not disclose commercial terms, transaction volumes, pricing or a target for payment corridors to be activated at launch.

Market context

Cross-border remittance and business payment infrastructure in East Africa is a competitive and increasingly well-funded space. Mobile-first providers, specialist remittance operators and pan-African payment networks are all vying for the outbound corridor from Uganda, which sees significant flows tied to diaspora remittances, trade finance and educational payments. The Bank of Uganda has maintained a relatively open licensing posture toward payment service providers, and the corridor into Uganda is already served by several international money transfer operators and mobile money platforms.

TerraPay’s strategic differentiator is positioning itself as a wholesale infrastructure layer for regulated institutions rather than competing directly with consumer-facing remittance brands. That approach sidesteps the customer-acquisition cost of building a retail brand but depends on signing banks and financial institutions that have the trust and distribution that TerraPay itself does not provide. The Exim Bank Uganda partnership fits that model, though Exim Bank’s relatively modest branch footprint and agent network means volume potential is meaningful but not transformative on TerraPay’s global scale.

For Exim Bank Uganda, the more important question is competitive parity with larger Ugandan commercial banks, several of which already offer international payment services through their own correspondent banking arrangements or through rival infrastructure providers. Whether Exim Global Pay competes on price, speed or convenience will determine how quickly it gains traction with the business customers who represent the higher-value segment of outbound cross-border flows.

Regulatory compliance for cross-border payments in Uganda falls under the Bank of Uganda’s National Payment Systems Act framework, and TerraPay holds licences across multiple jurisdictions. The release did not specify the regulatory approvals underpinning the new product in Uganda specifically.

fullText:
Quantum computing will bring significant opportunities to the UK financial sector, but firms need to act now to prepare for a world where a viable hostile quantum computer could break today’s widely used cryptography standards.

The financial sector depends on secure information and communication. Cryptography – of which encryption is just one part – helps firms protect their clients’ data, verify who they are dealing with, and maintain trust in their systems.

Sufficiently powerful quantum computers pose a real threat to that security. Without trustworthy cryptography, consumers would face fraud, firms would suffer operational disruption, and the integrity of financial transactions and markets would be put at risk.

That’s why we are talking to firms about preparing for post-quantum cryptography (PQC) now. We don’t know for certain when a viable quantum computer will emerge, but the coming years will likely see the technology advance at a rapid pace.

Preparing for this new world requires firms to understand where and how they use cryptography and to be able to migrate all hardware and software to PQC, while managing operational risks.

Realistically, for most firms, this will require significant time, investment and effort.

What firms need to do now

So, what kind of timescale are we talking about? The National Centre for Cyber Security (NCSC) recommends 3 key milestones:

By 2028, firms complete a PQC migration plan.

By 2031, firms carry out high-priority migration activities.

By 2035, firms have migrated all systems, services and products to PQC.

Firms should not wait for these milestones before acting and where it is safe to do so, they should seek to be ready sooner. In line with NCSC guidance, we expect firms to act now to: 

Have a thorough and accurate understanding of the cryptography in place across systems and information.

Set clear, achievable, safe and risk-based migration objectives..

Implement migration plans and monitor, test and validate the changes, adjusting them where necessary.

Senior managers should ensure that their firms allocate enough time, investment and resources to manage PQC migration safely and meet the relevant deadlines. Failed change projects accounted for around a fifth of all incidents reported to us in 2025.

How we are supporting firms

We are trialling a new supervisory self-assessment tool with an initial sample of firms and intend to extend it to other firms in due course. This will help firms assess the maturity of their plans and help us understand the industry’s preparedness for PQC migration.

This trial will also help us identify common challenges and examples of good practice, which we intend to share with the sector.

We shared relevant insights from firms in April 2026 and will continue to engage with the industry through our Cyber Coordination Groups (CCGs), the Cross Market Operational Resilience Group (CMORG), and trade bodies and associations.

We will also consult on cyber resilience guidance for firms, including our expectations for how firms should address PQC risks through their cryptographic controls.

title: Europe’s single market still has borders
snippet: how a business can localise its financial operations in a new market, without rebuilding them every time. The post Europe’s single market still has borders appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
With international expansion coming earlier and earlier in a business’ growth strategy, Vivien Cheung, Senior Director of Strategic Banking Partnerships at Airwallex, explains how a business can localise its financial operations in a new market, without rebuilding them every time. 

The expansion plan is ready: pricing, hiring, a launch date. Then the first payment doesn’t arrive.

The payer’s system had taken one look at the account details and flagged them with an error. That’s where the borders turn up. Not at a checkpoint, but in a payment system that doesn’t recognise the account.

Europe may appear like one market to a multinational business planning its next move, and it’s also why the gaps are so easy to miss. Banking arrangements, payment habits and regulators’ expectations still differ country by country. A failed payment is only the visible symptom, behind it sit accounts, entities and currencies that don’t necessarily line up.

I’ve supported customers through various market launches, and this pattern is consistent. Businesses spend months perfecting their entry and almost no time on what happens next. The EU’s single market opens the door to European trade, but it doesn’t do the operational work. As AI agents take on more of the finance function, that gap will only widen.

Localising to reuse not rebuild

The finance stack needs to ensure customers can pay the way they expect, suppliers can be paid without friction, and finance teams can see it all in one place.

In the Netherlands, an Airwallex customer can have a local Dutch IBAN, access to SEPA credit transfers, instant payments and direct debits, payment through iDEAL or Wero, a locally issued card and one view across every entity and currency. Each removes a small point of friction. Together, they separate a business that looks local from one that only sells there. Local regulation matters just as much. Every country has its own regulator with its own expectations, and it’s far better to learn them before you arrive than after. But tackle each one in isolation and localisation becomes fragmentation, with every country ending up as its own product.

A small business doesn’t need to become a specialist in local banking and regulation just because it scaled internationally. The goal instead should be to work from a core system that can be reused in each new market, then decide deliberately where to localise on top of it.

Connected systems are a growth decision

Every new market can add another account, another provider, and another set of records. When those systems don’t talk to each other, finance teams reconcile manually, and a failure can take days to trace back to its source. IMF research notes that Europe’s retail payments systems remain largely segmented even within national borders, which can impede small firms’ ability to scale beyond their home market.

At Airwallex, we chose to build our own infrastructure, acquiring 85+ licenses over a decade, which our founder and CEO, Jack Zhang, calls the ‘Path of Max Resistance’. It may have taken us longer to start, but it made sense in the long-run to build the core foundations that run global payments. Businesses want their financial operations to run on one system, with money moving reliably and instantly, which is much harder to guarantee across a chain of providers’ and their fragmented systems.

Now that our core infrastructure rails are in place, we are adding the global intelligence layer on top. The focus for each new market is about localising, not rebuilding. Localising doesn’t mean going it alone: the right partners still give us the local reach and the trust that every new market demands.

Readiness is organisational

The technology stack is the obvious place to start when asking whether you’re ready for the next market. Experience has taught me to check something less exciting: whether your teams are aligned behind one goal and know who is accountable for delivering it.

Expansion is one of the most cross-functional things a company will do. Product, finance, legal, compliance and operations all depend on each other, and one blocked workstream soon holds up three others. Three questions are worth stress-testing before launch. Does the end-to-end experience feel like one product? Is it clear what is strategically important to control? And who can make the final call when workstreams collide?

One of my biggest learnings is to invest in project management before it’s needed, and to give the team the mandate and seniority to drive decisions, not just track them. A ten-person business won’t have a project team, but it can name one person with that authority and a clear route to escalate. Each launch should leave behind processes the next one can reuse.

Agents raise the stakes

AI agents don’t change the fundamentals of expansion, they raise the stakes. When payments and financial decisions happen at agentic speed, the gaps a human team could work around become failures. A finance manager can step in and fix a problem manually, but an agent can’t. If your payments depend on several third parties, it inherits every handoff, delay, and dependency.

Knowing who controls the core infrastructure, such as how money moves and how risk and compliance are managed, is critical. It decides whether or not agents run on one consistent system. The model that works is one where people set the objectives and rules, and agents act within them. These foundations will determine if a business can keep up.

There is a significant opportunity for small businesses as agents make it easier to operate internationally, and I’m confident the businesses that win will be the ones whose infrastructure was built to support that from the start. At Airwallex, our goal is to give small businesses access to the sophisticated infrastructure of a global company, wherever their home market or whatever their headcount.

The expansion plan is the easy part. What decides whether that first payment arrives is the infrastructure underneath it.

title: Pine Labs and WEBXPAY Launch UPI Acceptance Across Sri Lanka
snippet: The PA-on-PA partnership, the first of its kind under India's RBI-authorised PA-CB framework, lets Sri Lankan merchants accept UPI, cards The post Pine Labs and WEBXPAY Launch UPI Acceptance Across Sri Lanka appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Pine Labs and Sri Lanka-based payment platform WEBXPAY have gone live with a cross-border payments partnership that enables Indian payment methods, including UPI, UPI AutoPay, net banking across more than 100 banks, major card networks, EMI conversions and Credit on UPI, to be accepted at Sri Lankan merchants. The arrangement is described by the two companies as the first Payment Aggregator-to-Payment Aggregator collaboration under India’s Reserve Bank of India-authorised PA-CB framework.

The PA-CB (Payment Aggregator Cross-Border) structure allows licensed Indian payment aggregators to partner directly with international counterparts, routing Indian payment rails into overseas markets within a regulated framework. Settlement operates on a T+1 basis, and the integration is embedded within WEBXPAY’s existing merchant infrastructure, meaning Sri Lankan businesses do not need to rework their payment stack to go live.

Why the framework matters

Tanya Naik, senior EVP and head of online business at Pine Labs

The PA-CB framework is a meaningful regulatory development in India’s approach to internationalising its payments infrastructure. Rather than requiring individual bilateral arrangements at the bank level, it creates a standardised pathway for licensed aggregators to extend their rails outward. The result is that a product like UPI, which processed billions of domestic transactions and achieved near-universal merchant penetration in India, can now be offered in international markets through a compliant, scalable wrapper rather than an ad hoc technical integration.

Thilak Piyadigama, executive chairman of WEBXPAY

Tanya Naik, senior executive vice president and head of online business at Pine Labs, said the company intends to replicate the model across Southeast Asia and every market where Indian travellers and consumers represent a significant commercial force. Sri Lanka is the first activation under this framework, with further markets signalled but not yet named.

Thilak Piyadigama, executive chairman of WEBXPAY, framed the commercial case directly: “Indian customers already know and trust payment methods such as UPI, cards and net banking. Bringing that familiarity into the online checkout experience of Sri Lankan merchants can remove a significant point of friction and help businesses convert more Indian demand into revenue.”

Market context and competitive read-across

The timing reflects genuine commercial logic. Sri Lanka received more than 530,000 Indian tourists in 2025, making India the country’s largest source market by volume, and that flow is continuing into 2026. Checkout abandonment driven by unfamiliar payment options is a well-documented problem in cross-border travel commerce, and the completion-rate uplift from presenting a recognised domestic payment method is measurable rather than theoretical.

More broadly, this partnership sits within a wider competition to extend UPI’s geographic reach. The National Payments Corporation of India has already pursued bilateral UPI acceptance agreements across the Gulf, Southeast Asia and parts of Europe, typically through interoperability arrangements rather than the PA-CB structure. The Pine Labs model is distinct in that it operates through a licensed aggregator layer rather than a direct interoperability link, which may prove easier to scale commercially across markets where NPCI has not yet formalised a bilateral deal.

For WEBXPAY, whose merchant base spans hospitality, travel, retail and online commerce, the partnership adds a high-intent consumer segment with an existing preference for specific payment rails. The commercial risk is largely on the Indian side: Pine Labs is taking on the regulatory overhead of PA-CB compliance and the settlement infrastructure required to make T+1 work across two currencies.

The partnership is explicitly positioned as a template. Whether the model can be replicated in higher-complexity markets, where local regulation, currency controls or incumbent payment networks create more friction, will determine whether PA-CB becomes a meaningful internationalisation vehicle or remains a niche corridor product.

title: SFF 2026: Five Forces Set to Rewire Global Finance
snippet: With one week to go, Singapore FinTech Festival 2026 convenes global leaders from 18–20 November to examine five forces rewiring finance: technology, geoeconomics, capital, talent, and policy. The post SFF 2026: Five Forces Set to Rewire Global Finance appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
With just one week remaining before the global financial technology community descends on Southeast Asia, final preparations are underway for the Singapore FinTech Festival (SFF) 2026. Taking place from 18 to 20 November 2026 at the Singapore EXPO, the flagship summit will convene central bankers, financial regulators, technology pioneers, institutional investors, and enterprise executives to navigate the structural transformations redefining international finance.

Organized by the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) and the Global Finance & Technology Network (GFTN), in collaboration with the Association of Banks in Singapore (ABS), SFF 2026 provides a high-level public-private platform to exchange strategic insights, forge cross-border partnerships, and shape regulatory architecture.

Five Structural Forces Rewiring Global Finance

This year’s edition centers on five interconnected macroeconomic and technological drivers that are reshaping financial systems worldwide:

Technology: As artificial intelligence accelerates productivity and economic growth, discussions will explore how financial institutions can deploy intelligent infrastructure while defending against sophisticated AI-enabled fraud, escalating cyber threats, and future quantum decryption vulnerabilities.

Geoeconomics: With global trade patterns fragmenting, cross-border investment flows shifting, and new commercial corridors emerging, sessions will analyze how cross-border clearing networks must adapt to sustain trade liquidity and systemic resilience.

Capital: Amid an unprecedented surge that has propelled AI-connected enterprises to approximately 40 per cent of the S&P 500’s total market capitalization, market participants will debate whether real revenue gains and enterprise productivity can sustainably justify current market valuations.

Talent: As autonomous systems and machine learning reconfigure organizational hierarchies and job functions, panels will address strategies for upskilling banking talent to maintain competitiveness in an AI-native operational landscape.

Policy: Regulators and legal architects will examine how compliance, supervisory governance, and systemic risk frameworks can keep pace with rapid innovation without compromising user protection, market integrity, and institutional trust.

Specialized Stage Programming and Capital Mobilization

Across the three-day main festival, SFF 2026 will host dedicated programs engineered to facilitate capital allocation, platform debuts, and executive engagement:

Founders Peak™: TED-inspired presentations where fintech founders deliver frank assessments of their entrepreneurial journeys, structural pivots, and operational lessons.

Investor Hours™ & Capital Meets Policy Dialogue™: Closed-door sessions connecting institutional allocators, venture capitalists, startup founders, and policymakers to pressure-test business models and unlock cross-border capital.

SFF MeetUp™: Asia’s largest structured fintech networking platform, designed to drive targeted, pre-scheduled business introductions across banking, payment infrastructure, and digital assets.

The Global FinTech Hackcelerator™: A showcase for early-stage innovators addressing complex industry challenges, featuring dedicated mentorship, venture capital access, and a Demo Day prize pool.

Multi-Hall Exhibition & International Pavilions: An expansive exhibition featuring cutting-edge infrastructure providers, incumbent financial institutions, and specialized national delegations from across the globe.

Insights2040 Annual Meeting to Anchor Pre-Festival Dialogue

Ahead of the main festival doors opening at Singapore EXPO, MAS and GFTN will host the Insights2040 Annual Meeting (IAM)—formerly known as the Insights Forum—from 16 to 17 November at the Sands Expo & Convention Centre.

The invite-only symposium brings together senior global public and private sector leaders for two days of collaborative problem-solving. Held under Chatham House rules, the closed-door working groups will address pressing cross-sector priorities, spanning sovereign digital infrastructure, tokenized real-world assets, quantum security, and ethical AI deployment.

Delegate registration for the Singapore FinTech Festival remains open via the official festival portal, with complimentary passes available for government officials, central banks, regulators, multilateral agencies, academics, and non-profit institutions.

title: Card Networks Use B2B Payments to Write the Rules for Agentic Commerce
snippet: Business payments have a bookkeeping problem that’s been keeping them manual for centuries. Millennia, even. In 2026, after one company approves an invoice, someone often must authenticate into a supplier portal, enter payment credentials and complete the transaction. Even two digitally native, forward-thinking CFOs doing business with one another can find it challenging to streamline […] The post Card Networks Use B2B Payments to Write the Rules for Agentic Commerce appeared first on PYMNTS.com.
fullText:
Business payments have a bookkeeping problem that’s been keeping them manual for centuries. Millennia, even.

In 2026, after one company approves an invoice, someone often must authenticate into a supplier portal, enter payment credentials and complete the transaction. Even two digitally native, forward-thinking CFOs doing business with one another can find it challenging to streamline and scale the need to authenticate and reconcile high-value and sensitive B2B payments.

Agentic AI, however, might just hold a long-awaited solution. One that the payments and FinTech marketplace is rapidly working toward. On Monday (Nov. 9), for example, payments technology company Clink added support for Mastercard Agent Pay, adding to its existing Visa Intelligent Commerce capabilities.

The development follows an October Visa initiative involving both BILL and Billtrust which allowed authenticated AI agents to complete previously approved invoice payments through supplier portals.

Both initiatives address some of B2B’s most stubbornly manual elements. And while AI can eliminate many final interventions across payments, doing so introduces more consequential questions, such as who authenticates the agent, defines its spending authority and assumes responsibility when an automated payment goes wrong?

Card networks like Visa and Mastercard are moving to establish the infrastructure that answers those questions.

Read more: Why the Fed Thinks B2B Payments Are Already Built for Agentic 

Authorization Becomes the New B2B Payment Battleground

For decades, payment networks have competed over acceptance, transaction volume and the economics of moving money. Agentic commerce adds a new competitive layer: establishing whether a machine has permission to initiate a transaction.

“Authentication remains foundational in an AI landscape,”  Chris Trainor, head of platform strategy, innovation and AI at Paymentus, told PYMNTS in an earlier discussion of agentic AI and payments. “The mistake that many have is expecting that model itself to become the system of record or a transaction processing engine. The future is not unconstrained artificial intelligence. It is governed agency.”

The operational advantage of card networks isn’t that they process payments but that, in doing so, they already operate the credentials, authentication systems and commercial rules connecting banks, buyers and suppliers. The important distinction is that the agent isn’t deciding whether the invoice should be paid. It’s executing a payment decision already made by the business.

Automating execution allows companies to preserve established approval processes. Delegating payment decisions introduces substantially more complicated questions about corporate authority, fraud and liability. For now, the networks are concentrating on the first opportunity of making existing financial instructions executable by trusted software.

Read more: AI Agents Need Permissioned Funding Sources. Not Company Bank Accounts. 

Clink’s integration with both Mastercard and Visa highlights an emerging competitive dynamic. Mastercard’s Agent Pay initiative, similar to Visa’s, combine tokenized credentials, authentication and transaction controls to support payments initiated by AI agents.

The PYMNTS Intelligence report “How Agentic AI Went From Zero to CFO Test Runs in 90 Days“ found in September 2025 that nearly 7% of enterprise CFOs in the U.S. had deployed agentic AI in live finance workflows, while an additional 5% were running pilots.

Software developers want the ability to build purchasing experiences without being confined to one payment network. The networks, meanwhile, want their credentials and authorization capabilities embedded wherever those experiences operate.

An enterprise software provider might determine when an invoice is ready for settlement. A bank might provide the funding. A card network might authenticate the agent and enable the transaction. A supplier platform might determine whether the payment can be accepted. Each participant has an opportunity to control a different part of the workflow.

The networks are attempting to make authorization their indispensable contribution.

Read more: Agentic AI Could Make Net 30 Obsolete

Banks Could Win Even as Payment Decisions Move Into Software

The early advantage of card networks doesn’t mean banks are losing relevance. In fact, agentic payments could make banks more valuable, provided their products and controls are embedded in automated workflows.

Banks already supply the credit, operating accounts, liquidity services and financial relationships that underpin corporate payments. As agents begin selecting payment methods, those capabilities could become inputs.

“Payment execution alone is increasingly commoditized. The durable value as I see it today is in making the right payment decisions,”  Tungsten Automation Head of Payments and Embedded Finance Andrew Ng told PYMNTS for the September edition of the “What’s Next in Payments Series: The Fall Draft.”

An agent might eventually choose between a commercial card and an account-to-account transfer based on supplier acceptance costs, available credit, cash flow requirements or payment terms.

Of course, making agents recognizable to payment networks solves only part of the problem.

A properly authenticated agent can still execute an incorrect payment. For CFOs, that means the economic case for agentic payments must also account for exception handling, payment recovery, dispute resolution and the cost of maintaining controls across multiple software and financial providers.

The companies that solve those problems could establish a competitive advantage that extends beyond transaction processing.

title: BNPL for rent seeks a market
snippet: A new crop of fintechs is exploring growth opportunities in pay-later lending for monthly rent payments as inflation pinches consumers.
fullText:
Pay-later loans are increasingly available for monthly housing payments as financial technology companies seek growth by responding to consumers’ affordability struggles.

While the buy now, pay later market has traditionally focused on providing consumers with financing at retail merchants for discretionary items, a newer batch of companies sees profit potential in tailoring loans to rental payments and other monthly bills such as utilities, medical care and telephone service.

A variety of players have moved into the pay-later rental arena in recent years, aiming to fill financial gaps between consumers’ monthly rents and their incomes, as the increases in the former outpace the latter.

Ariel Nelson

Permission granted by National Consumer Law Center

The rise of these businesses is “really revealing in what they say about the state of affordability around life essentials,” said Ariel Nelson, a senior attorney with the National Consumer Law Center. “These products are really appealing because people are desperate.”

Companies seeking to develop a market in the rental area include RealPage, an apartment management software firm, which last year bought Livble, a startup that offers renters flexible payment options. Another is New York-based Flexible Finance, known as Flex, which lets consumers split their rent, mortgage or other monthly bill payments. 

A third rent-focused fintech is Bilt Technologies, which offers a payments and loyalty program aimed at attracting rent and mortgage payments to credit cards, including its co-branded cards. In addition to points for rent and everyday spending on cards, New York-based Bilt issues points for homeowners’ association and condominium fee payments.

Bilt members can transfer the points to 18 airline and seven hotel loyalty partner programs to redeem for flights and hotel stays. The points can also be redeemed at merchants such as Amazon.com and Lyft.

Consumer advocates contend that pay-later products aimed at rent and medical care can exacerbate financial strains for economically vulnerable people and lead to a stacking of their debt.

“As the price of shelter has shot up, a new breed of predatory creditors has emerged aiming to turn this emergency into profit,” advocacy group Protect Borrowers said in a February report on the rent now, pay later industry. “Beneath the surface, these products are united in being little more than a repackaging of an age-old debt trap: payday loans.”

About 109 million Americans have a monthly rental payment, according to Protect Borrowers, a Washington-based nonprofit that lobbies and litigates on consumer debt issues. The group was formed in 2018 as the Student Borrower Protection Center by former officials of the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau. 

Pay-later options allow renters to avoid being late on their rent, avoiding landlords’ late fees and revolving credit card interest rates that can reach 30% or more, Zahir Khoja, RealPage’s chief fintech officer, said in an interview last month. The average late fee is $85, he said.

“It’s not that you can’t pay your rent,” he said of tenant customers that select pay-later plans. “You may not be able to pay your rent on January 1st, and so you need some time in the month of January to be able to do it. It’s much better than paying a late fee or revolving at 29.9 (percent) on credit.”

Another BNPL provider, Sydney-based Zip, offers a bill-payment service to split monthly bills such as insurance, utilities and mobile phone. The company is also exploring a new rent-focused service for the U.S. market. 

Many “everyday Americans” are challenged by a misalignment between the timing of their income and bills, Zip’s former U.S. CEO, Joe Heck, told analysts on the BNPL provider’s August earnings call. Heck left Zip last month, the company said in an Oct. 16 investor announcement.

“Most consumers are paid every two weeks, while bills like rent are generally due monthly,” Heck said. “That mismatch in timing of income and expenses creates large opportunities beyond BNPL,” he said, pointing to bill payments and the need for “income-smoothing” as other ways the services could be used. 

Shragie Lichtenstein

Permission granted by Flex

The U.S. monthly rent and bill market is a $2 trillion addressable opportunity, compared to $160 billion for the retail BNPL market, Zip said in its investor presentation.

“I do think that this is a trend, both for rent and in general consumer essentials, that’s likely to continue,” Flex co-founder and CEO Shragie Lichtenstein said in an interview Oct. 8. 

Competing payment plans

RealPage, which is based in suburban Dallas, sells property-management software and rent payment financing services. The company offers both Livble and Flex via its app for residents and property managers or owners. 

Despite its Livble ownership, RealPage promotes both brands with its property owner customers, Khoja said. “We tell them ‘Hey, it’s Pepsi (or) Coke. Let the customer decide which one works for them.’”

Flex is a subscription service for tenants that collects a percentage of the rent as a payment for the service, he said Oct. 18, during an interview at the Money20/20 financial technology conference in Las Vegas. “Whereas ours (Livble) is just a flat fee, so it’s different – whatever works for you better as the resident.”

Another difference is that Flex offers credit cards as a payment method, while Livble accepts only ACH, said Khoja, who joined RealPage in March. 

Livble charges customers a fee for each payment they make, eschewing recurring monthly membership or subscription fees. Livble’s typical payment fee is $30 to $35 but are “nuanced by state,” which is why they’re not posted on the company’s website, a RealPage spokesperson said last week in an email. A resident using Livble, “will always know the fee before it’s final,” the spokesperson said. The company didn’t immediately respond to a question about how it presents its fees to customers. 

“We don’t want you to get into perpetual debt,” Khoja said. “Our goal is to actually help you go up the financial-inclusion ladder, where you’re now able to stand on your own two feet and do things without revolving credit at such high rates or taking third-party loans that you can’t repay.”

A playground at an apartment complex in Irving, Texas, near Dallas.

Getty Images

Two years ago, the Justice Department and eight states filed an antitrust lawsuit alleging that RealPage helped apartment owners collude to fix rental prices. The lawsuit said that the company’s pricing software used nonpublic, sensitive data collected from apartment owners to develop rental rate recommendations in various markets and keep rents higher than they would have been in a competitive market.

The company and government settled the case last year, with RealPage agreeing to stop using sensitive information from landlords to determine the rental prices that it suggested through its software. The company did not admit or deny wrongdoing or face a financial penalty as part of the agreement. Several antitrust lawsuits filed by states and private plaintiffs continue. Private equity firm Thoma Bravo acquired RealPage in 2021. 

Another rent-payment focused startup, New York-based Esusu, has partnered with BNPL provider Affirm Holdings to allow renters to split their rent into two equal payments. The Esusu program remains an “early-stage pilot” in testing and consists only of evenly split rent payments, with no fees or interest, an Affirm spokesperson said last month in an email.

Esusu charges a $59 membership fee, paid monthly or annually, depending on whether a tenant’s apartment property is part of the company’s network. The company also has a “split pay” program allowing renters to pay 60% of their rent upfront and divide the remainder into two or three payments. Esusu did not respond to a message seeking comment on its business model. 

Determining the costs of these rent-payment programs “can be confusing,” said Nelson, the NCLC attorney, noting that such information is often buried deep within user terms and conditions.

“I cannot for the life of me figure out how much they cost,” she said of having looked around different pay-later providers’ websites for pricing information. “And that’s also a problem.”

Scattered regulatory oversight

Pay-later lending has had little oversight at the federal level. Several states – including Illinois, New York and Oregon – have formulated rules to regulate the industry as the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau has contracted during the Trump administration. 

In June, U.S. Rep. Daniel Goldman, a Democrat from New York City, introduced a bill to apply the federal Truth in Lending Act to BNPL loans, effectively regulating them as credit cards. The measure hasn’t moved beyond the House Financial Services Committee, according to Congress’ website.

BNPL “users have been left with no federal protections,” Goldman said in a press release announcing his bill, referring to the CFPB’s decision to retreat last year from a 2024 decision to regulate pay-later loans much like credit cards.

Another bill, filed by Sen. Jack Reed, a Rhode Island Democrat, would amend the Truth in Lending law, which dates to the late 1960s, and the 2010 Consumer Financial Protection Act to apply new oversight and consumer protections. Reed’s legislation, filed late last year, has attracted four Democratic co-sponsors and a companion bill in the House, but no Republican sponsors, according to Congress.gov.

Lichtenstein, the Flex CEO, said that one challenge facing the RNPL industry is that these products “don’t fit into a clean box” neatly for regulators to evaluate what they are and how they work.

“The more you don’t fit into a clean box, the more regulatory scrutiny it draws,” he said. “We have tried our best to fit into a relatively clean box,” he said, adding that the company has “internal guardrails” to help it evaluate “the many, many gray areas that can exist for consumer fintech.”

However, he added, pay-later services for rent differ from other financial services, often “embedded” with the rent payment and with different pricing models. 

The RNPL industry doesn’t currently have a “uniform set of standards” from regulators under which to operate, Lichtenstein said, which can lead to different practices among the various players. “Continued clarity on the right way to do things would be welcome by us,” he said.

Risks for renters?

Beyond high fees and the potential for debt accumulation, rent-payment services pose “a significant risk” to borrowers because lenders often link directly to consumers’ bank accounts and offer “disastrously poor customer service” in addressing errors or other account issues, according to the Protect Borrowers report. 

Their growth is also likely to lead to further regulatory scrutiny, with at least one state, New York, being encouraged by the New York City Department of Consumer and Worker Protection to apply its BNPL rules expansively to other providers in adjacent verticals. 

Pay-later services are marketed by lenders “who claim that these loans can ease the housing affordability or healthcare accessibility crisis,” Commissioner Samuel A.A. Levine of the New York City DCWP wrote in September in a letter to New York state financial regulators. “However, in both cases, these products fail to address the underlying problems and result only in consumers facing new and compounding risks.”

Among various recommendations to the state’s Department of Financial Services, Levine urged regulators to include “all forms of BNPL products” in its pending rules for such lenders, including those that offer rent payment services.

“The stakes are really high, so I think we need to be extremely cautious about how we handle products in this space.”

Ariel Nelson

National Consumer Law Center

Esusu raised $50 million last December. Its platform covers about 5 million rental units, with 12 million people, according to the company’s press release. The company also offers a rent-payment reporting service to help renters build their credit scores. 

Esusu says on its website that its credit services are needed because two-thirds of Americans “live paycheck to paycheck” and that about “30% of lower-income households spend 95% or more of their income on basic necessities like housing, food and utilities.”

Affirm doesn’t allow a consumer to borrow further if they have an outstanding balance from the prior month, Affirm’s vice president of government relations, John Pitts, wrote in a February blog post in response to the Protect Borrowers report, seeking to highlight differences between Affirm and others in the rent market.

“Being financially blindsided by hidden fees and/or still paying January’s rent in March is not solving affordability, it’s stacking debt,” Pitts wrote. “That’s why our products are structurally different.”

Regulators are beginning to “get educated in this space, and they're asking the right questions to provide the consumer protection around it,” said RealPage’s Khoja. Officials in states with the largest numbers of renters – California, Florida, New York and Texas – are among those gathering information about how RNPL firms work, he said.

However, the field of pay later for rent is nascent and state officials are still “catching up” with its growth, said Nelson, the consumer attorney.

“You’re talking about people who are doing whatever it takes to keep a roof over their head,” she said. “This isn’t like I couldn’t pay for an expensive pair of shoes – you could literally be homeless. The stakes are really high, so I think we need to be extremely cautious about how we handle products in this space.”
