title: Why a Zero Trust Approach Matters to Banking Resilience
snippet: QNB Group's chief information security officer on why being inside a bank's network should never be mistaken for trust, and how a decade of zero trust has shaped its resilience. The post Why a Zero Trust Approach Matters to Banking Resilience appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
The principle behind zero trust is straightforward. Being inside a bank’s network does not, by itself, make a user or device trustworthy. 

Dr Alex Constantinidis, Chief information security officer, QNB Group

Dr Alex Constantinidis is group chief information security officer of QNB Group. In this contributed piece he sets out QNB’s zero trust approach and what it has taught the bank about resilience, he explains how applying that discipline for almost a decade has shaped the way the bank contains a compromise, governs what leaves its network and prepares for change.

Access must be explicitly authorised and limited to what is needed. If an account, device or application is compromised, the security architecture should help contain the consequences.

That works in two directions. Looking inward, it governs what a potentially compromised account or system can reach once inside the network. Looking outward, it governs what employees and systems are allowed to reach beyond it. Both matter, and a bank’s resilience depends on applying the same discipline to each.

At QNB Group, a zero trust approach has guided both for almost a decade. It has shaped how we design our network security architecture to contain a potential compromise, and how we govern what connects outward from it, as our digital environment has evolved. That experience offers a practical perspective on a central responsibility for banks: expanding digital capabilities while protecting the institution’s systems, its employees and, by extension, the customers who depend on it.

For us, zero trust connects everyday security decisions with the Group’s long-term resilience and ability to adapt.

Containing a compromise

An airport offers a useful way to understand layered access. Entering the terminal does not entitle a traveller to go everywhere. Identity checks, security screening and restricted zones each serve a purpose, and additional authorisation is required to pass from landside to airside.

Passengers already inside the terminal are not assumed to be safe. They pass through further checkpoints that revalidate their identity and confirm they carry nothing dangerous before they board. Presence inside the perimeter is not treated as proof of trust.

Phishing remains the leading vector of compromise, and it illustrates why this matters. An attacker who phishes an employee does not break into the network; they are admitted to it, with the same level of access as the employee they are impersonating. The architecture must therefore assume that a legitimate identity can be misused, and limit what any single identity can reach.

In a digital environment, access to one resource should confer no automatic right to another. We combine access controls with segmentation and defined routes into sensitive systems to limit an attacker’s ability to move through the environment after an initial compromise.

The same thinking shapes the security architecture of our customer-facing applications. Their components are separated into distinct layers and placed in separate zones, each with its own controls on what can reach it. If one component is compromised, the attacker is contained within that zone and cannot easily move between layers to reach the systems and data behind it.

At QNB, this principle also shapes administrative access. Administrators access servers through a separate, controlled management environment with additional authentication. Separating administrative activity from everyday workstation use reduces the number of systems an attacker could reach through a single compromised device.

This reflects a realistic view of cybersecurity. New vulnerabilities can emerge in widely used technologies, so resilience requires attention to both prevention and containment. The question is not only how to prevent a compromise, but how effectively the institution can limit its impact and maintain operations if one occurs.

Controlling what leaves the network

Few online interactions involve only one party. When an employee opens a webpage, the browser connects not only to the site itself but also to the trackers, advertising networks and analytics services embedded in it. Each of these is a separate connection the user never sees. Governing access therefore means assessing these third-party dependencies alongside the primary service.

At QNB, employees request access to the external sites and services they need for their work, so that those requirements can be assessed before access is granted. This helps us distinguish connections that serve a business need from those that introduce unnecessary exposure.

For internet-based business applications, we analyse every dependency on external resources before access is granted. Many applications rely on shared public infrastructure, such as public storage services, and an access requirement that resolves to one of these can inadvertently open a route to the wider service. Permitting that route could allow data to be exfiltrated or allow an attacker to host malicious code behind a trusted domain name. We assess each requirement to ensure it is scoped to the service itself and does not extend to public resources beyond it.

Adapting through preparedness

Making zero trust work requires more than technical controls. Security teams must understand what employees need to accomplish and explain the reasons for access restrictions. Executive backing provides a consistent mandate and ensures that decisions reflect the Group’s agreed appetite for risk.

One of the clearest lessons from our experience is that zero trust becomes sustainable when it is embedded in how the organisation makes decisions. Technology provides the controls; leadership and operational processes sustain their effective use.

That consistency becomes particularly valuable as technology evolves. When our zero trust journey began, QNB’s environment was predominantly on premises. New services and technologies have since introduced different dependencies and access requirements, while the underlying principles have continued to guide how we assess and manage them.

Preparedness also means anticipating needs before they become urgent. Before Covid-19, we had established remote-access capabilities for a limited group of users. When the pandemic created a wider requirement for remote working, that provision gave us a foundation we could expand. It demonstrated the value of building security capabilities that support the Group’s ability to adapt to disruption.

A mature security foundation should allow new regulatory or certification obligations to be met through targeted enhancements rather than complete redesign, and should support new technologies and ways of working. Alongside the volume and severity of security incidents, this adaptability is one of the measures by which we assess the effectiveness of our cybersecurity programme.

Setting expectations for technology partners

These principles also inform how we assess business applications. A system holding public marketing information may appear less sensitive than one holding confidential customer data. Yet its permissions and connections to the wider environment still matter. An asset containing little sensitive information can still provide a route to something more valuable.

We therefore apply a strong, consistent security baseline, and assess each application on two counts: where it sits within the internal environment, and what it needs to reach outside it. Protecting the environment requires an understanding of how its parts interact.

Technology partners have an important responsibility here. Banks need clarity about a product’s external dependencies, its access requirements and its ability to operate within a controlled environment. A product whose dependencies cannot be clearly described cannot be properly assessed. These questions should be addressed early in the selection process, when they can still inform the decision to proceed. Where a product’s dependencies cannot be separated from shared public infrastructure, that limitation should be understood and weighed before adoption, not discovered afterwards.

This leads to a clear expectation: software products should be designed to work within an institution’s security architecture. If adopting a product requires established protections to be weakened, its design should be challenged and alternatives considered.

For QNB, almost a decade of applying zero trust has reinforced the value of consistent principles as banking technology changes. Understanding connections, controlling access and containing the impact of a compromise provide a foundation for adopting new capabilities with greater confidence. Financial institutions and their technology partners can strengthen that foundation by making compatibility with security requirements an expectation from the outset.

First Citizens Bank is partnering with NCR Atleos to offer surcharge-free access to services via ATMs located at some 2,000 Target stores, the bank said in a press release last month. As part of the agreement, the bank’s customers can use the ATMs at Target stores to withdraw cash, check their account balances and transfer funds to eligible linked accounts without paying a fee, according to the Oct. 19 release.

“The consumer banking experience needs to meet customers where they are through multiple channels, whether in-person or digitally enabled,” First Citizens Bank’s head of consumer banking, Michael Wilson, said in the release. 

Meanwhile, NCR Atleos CEO Tim Oliver said Wednesday that the company’s sale to Brink’s is progressing, with expected completion of the transaction by January.

Dive Insight:

For NCR Atleos, which became a standalone company three years ago, the partnership with First Citizens allows it to add new service providers to its roster. 

The company separated from its parent in late 2023, creating two publicly traded companies: NCR Voyix and NCR Atleos. While NCR Atleos offers ATMs and other interactive teller machines for payments and banking services, NCR Voyix offers point-of-sale hardware and related services to restaurant, retail and other merchants.

As NCR Atleos has grown its corporate clientele, including by working with American Express and PayNearMe in recent years, its self-service banking segment has bolstered revenue. The company reported third-quarter earnings results Wednesday that showed its self-service banking segment rose 3% to $2.17 billion for the first nine months of the year, faster than its overall business revenue growth, which increased 2% to $3.23 billion for the period, according to the earnings press release. 

“Our service-led growth initiatives and investment in product innovation are encouraging financial institutions and retailers to choose our differentiated and comprehensive offering to meet their evolving self-service needs,” Oliver said in August when the company reported second-quarter earnings. 

NCR’s partnership with First Citizens comes as the ATM provider prepares to be acquired. In February, the Brink’s Company agreed to buy NCR Atleos in a cash and stock transaction valued at about $6.6 billion. As part of the deal, Brink’s will also take on $2.6 billion in NCR Atleos debt, a press release on the transaction said. 

Regulators have yet to approve the deal. The Competition and Markets Authority in the U.K. said Brink’s acquisition of NCR Atleos could limit competition, according to a September report from the news outlet Reuters. Earlier this month, the Wall Street Journal reported Brink’s plans to sell some subsidiaries in a move aimed at assuaging U.K. concerns.

“We continue to make meaningful progress on regulatory approval processes across the multiple jurisdictions, and have significantly advanced the integration planning activities for the pending combination of Atleos and The Brink’s Company,” Oliver said in the release this week.

title: OCC Gives Bank Examiners a New Playbook for Reviewing AI
snippet: Banks are handing more work to artificial intelligence. Some AI tools now handle business activities like credit decisioning, customer service and fraud detection. That raises a simple question: Who makes sure these systems get it right? The nation’s top bank regulator offered its answer. The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency released Nov. 4 […] The post OCC Gives Bank Examiners a New Playbook for Reviewing AI appeared first on PYMNTS.com.
fullText:
Banks are handing more work to artificial intelligence.

Some AI tools now handle business activities like credit decisioning, customer service and fraud detection. That raises a simple question: Who makes sure these systems get it right? The nation’s top bank regulator offered its answer.

The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency released Nov. 4 the “OCC Supervisory Framework on Bank Use of Super Intelligence,” a new guide to help its examiners review how banks use AI.

The guide focuses on generative AI, which creates text and other content. It also covers agentic AI, which can take actions without a person stepping in each time. The OCC called this technology super intelligence, the term used by the executive branch in place of artificial intelligence, according to a Sept. 29 executive order signed by President Donald Trump.

The guide doesn’t create new rules for banks, according to an analysis from law firm Ballard Spahr. It’s a resource for the people who inspect them. Banks won’t have to treat AI as its own risk category. Examiners will instead look at how AI changes the risks banks already manage. These include fraud, privacy, cybersecurity and work with outside vendors.

The OCC built the guide around six areas, per the analysis. Examiners will ask what an AI system is allowed to do and what happens if it makes a mistake. They’ll look at the guardrails a bank has in place and who’s keeping watch. They’ll check how a bank recovers when a system fails. And they’ll want proof that the bank’s safety checks keep working over time.

The guide also said risk depends on how much freedom an AI system has, according to the analysis. A simple bot that can start payments may pose more danger than a powerful model that only helps staff draft memos. To sort this out, the OCC laid out four risk levels. Payment bots that act on their own and instant credit decisions sit at the top. Internal tools that never touch customer data sit at the bottom.

“[T]he more consequential and autonomous the activity, the more extensive the controls should be,” the analysis said.

Human review gets a close look, too. The OCC warned that a person who just clicks “approve” doesn’t count as real oversight. Reviewers need the skills, the facts and the power to reject or stop what the AI is doing, per the analysis.

Customers are a big focus. AI chatbots can give wrong answers about fees, interest rates or account balances. The OCC said these errors could lead to legal trouble and harm customers, according to the analysis. Banks can’t blame the machine, either. A bank is still on the hook if its AI breaks the law.

Many banks buy their AI from outside companies, so vendors face extra scrutiny, the analysis said. The guide asked whether contracts spell out who pays when an AI tool causes harm. It also asked whether vendors must warn banks before they change how their AI works. A vendor could add new AI features to an old product, and the bank might not notice the new risks.

So, what comes next? In a bulletin released with the guide, the OCC said the document sets no binding standards. Banks aren’t even expected to use it to grade their own AI programs.

Still, the analysis said banks shouldn’t ignore it. The guide offers a clear preview of what examiners may ask about during future bank exams. Banks should study it closely and check whether their current risk and compliance programs already cover the issues the OCC raised. Banks that find gaps now may have an easier time when examiners come calling.

Block subsidiary Cash App has partnered with luxury apparel and footwear brand Nahmias to create a bandana that enables digital payments, the Oakland, California-based peer-to-peer payments provider said in a Monday press release.

The bandana has the payment company’s tap-to-pay tag, which lets customers pay without using their phones or wallets. The cotton and silk bandana features Cash App’s patch woven in a corner, indicating where users can tap to make contactless payments, the release said.

The two companies will begin selling the accessory exclusively through Cash App for $85 starting Nov. 17, per the release.

Dive Insight:

With its Nahmias partnership, Block, Cash App’s parent company, is continuing to experiment with unusual payment tools. In June, the company introduced its digital wand, which enables payments using its digital payment tags attached to wand-like keychains with stars at the end, the company said in an earlier release.

“Working with Cash App gave us the opportunity to reimagine an everyday accessory as a new way to pay, while putting our own Nahmias language on the design,” founder and creative director of the namesake brand, Doni Nahmias, said in the release. “We wanted to create something that feels effortless to wear and style, but also has a practical purpose.”

As Cash App expands its payment capabilities to uncommon objects, digital wallets are extending their offerings beyond cardless payments. And it’s not the only payments player to tap inanimate objects as payment tools: tech company Apple offers Apple Pay options for its proprietary watches.

Payment players like Google and Apple are allowing for personal documents to be tucked into digital wallets, letting users carry virtual driver’s licenses, passports, airline boarding passes and concert tickets. 

Along with integrating more personal documents into digital wallets, payment companies are increasingly relying on biometrics to execute transactions. Earlier this year, Clover, the Fiserv subsidiary, began providing its biometric verification services to Fiserv merchants, enabling consumers to pay with their face and palms.

fullText:
FinTechs are expanding their lending businesses from two places customers already visit: the app where their paychecks land and the card they bring to the store.

Two examples have jumped out recently. Chime is testing a credit line for customers who deposit at least $3,000 a month to qualify for Prime. Affirm’s debit card is bringing its installment loans to purchases outside the merchant checkouts where it has signed agreements.

Chime reported higher losses during its third-quarter earnings results Nov. 4 as more Prime members borrowed for the first time, while Affirm said as part of its first-quarter fiscal year 2027 earnings results Thursday (Nov. 5) that it typically earns less from the merchant side of a card transaction than from a checkout integration.

“On average, the interchange that we collect is probably lower than the average merchant discount rate that we would have through an integrated merchant,” Affirm Chief Financial Officer Rob O’Hare said during an earnings call. More than 80% of loans made through Affirm Card historically carried interest. Cardholders also make purchases that they pay in full.

Affirm’s earnings presentation counted 6 million cardholders who had used the card at least once in the preceding year, about 21% of its active customers. About 30% of card transactions took place in stores, and arranging installments before the purchase remained the most common use, CEO Max Levchin said. He also described approaching retailers after their customers had already used the card at their stores. A direct agreement lets a retailer extend its subsidized financing offers to cardholders as well as shoppers who select Affirm at checkout.

Affirm plans to introduce card-specific financing offers this quarter and is preparing to pilot Edge, which would make its installment loans available through other issuers’ debit cards, in the first half of 2027.

For lenders issuing cards, the competition continues after sign-up. The PYMNTS Intelligence report “The Rewards Gap: Turning Member Interest Into Growth” found in November that 40% of consumers with multiple cards cited better incentives, including cash back, as a factor in choosing which card to use.

Separately, the PYMNTS Intelligence report “Beyond Pay in 4: Many BNPL Buyers Would Pay for More Time” found in August that 82% of buy now, pay later users with four or more providers said they would pay interest for a longer repayment term, compared with 46% of those who used one provider.

From Deposits to Loans

Chime uses the deposits and spending it sees in customer accounts to decide how much to lend. People earning at least $75,000 were its fastest-growing group of new sign-ups.

“Among these members, a significantly higher share are direct-depositing and qualifying for Prime by depositing $3,000 or more per month,” CEO Chris Britt said on the Nov. 4 earnings call.

Chime originated $381 million in Instant Loans during the quarter. President and Interim Chief Financial Officer Mark Troughton said first-time borrowing by Prime members contributed to the rise in losses. Annualized loss rates for repeat borrowers were up to 50% lower than for first-time borrowers. Chime also introduced joint accounts and made investing available to all members, according to its earnings release.

Cash App’s numbers put the size of an app’s payment audience in perspective. Block reported 60 million Cash App accounts that transacted in September, compared with 9.4 million that met its primary banking definition, which held steady from June. The second group includes accounts with eligible wage inflows as well as accounts that qualify by spending at least $500 a month through Cash App services.

At Robinhood, the brokerage account itself is a source of deposits. CEO Vlad Tenev said Robinhood Banking received more money from Robinhood brokerage withdrawals than any other destination during the quarter. Opening a banking account still required a brokerage account.

At SoFi, existing members accounted for more than half of the products opened in the quarter. Its Oct. 27 earnings release counted services such as Relay, which tracks spending and monitors credit scores, alongside banking and investing products.

title: How Barclays tucked into Samsung
snippet: Twenty-plus years into card co-brands, Barclays’ newest launch – a card integrated into Samsung’s digital wallet – offers both new challenges and opportunities.
fullText:
When Barclays entered the U.S. credit card market in 2004, it bet on a partnership model to set itself apart from competitors.

Twenty-two years later, a co-branded card originally started by the bank it acquired – the Frontier Airlines credit card, started by Juniper Bank in 2003 – is going strong. The partnership was extended in June, through 2037.

In July, Barclays launched another co-brand: the Samsung Galaxy Card, which integrates into the Samsung wallet when a customer is approved. (The card also has the potential to be its most far-reaching, as according to Samsung, one in seven people worldwide have a Galaxy phone. About 30% of U.S. smartphone users are Samsung Galaxy customers, according to Counterpoint Research.)

Launching this product was different than Barclays’ other co-brand products, in part because of an added “layer of coordination” between the bank and its partner, said Doug Villone, head of U.S. cards and partnerships at Barclays’ U.S. consumer bank. But the effort is paying off as adoption numbers are promising, according to Villone.

Villone explored this and other topics last month with Banking Dive at the Money20/20 conference in Las Vegas.

Editor’s note: This interview has been edited for clarity and brevity.

BANKING DIVE: You said adoption of the Samsung partnership was ahead of expectations. By what measure, and how far ahead?

DOUG VILLONE: Something you worry about when you launch a new co-brand, especially one with a very strong value proposition within the partner's properties, is that the card ends up being used to buy a phone [in Samsung’s case] but doesn't get used to buy your coffee.

We can’t share specific customer sign-up figures, but adoption has exceeded our internal business-case expectations. More than half of transactions are made through Samsung Pay, and most of those are outside Samsung’s own ecosystem. That suggests customers are using the card for everyday purchases, not just buying Samsung products. Overall, customer activity, spending and adoption have met or exceeded expectations so far.

Has customer feedback led to changes since launch?

We never viewed this as a “set it and forget it” product. We expect to add features and functionality over time. Currently, customers can complete about 70% of common servicing tasks in the Samsung Wallet, including making payments, viewing transactions and redeeming rewards. We’re not satisfied with that. 

There are still things that you might need to contact Barclays about, and we want to continue to make it so ultimately, you never have to leave the Samsung Wallet ecosystem to do that. We offer loans and deposits and other things to consumers in our other programs, and I can imagine a world where there would be more things that would be available to [Samsung Galaxy card] consumers as well – things like servicing chat, which we think would be a great add-on feature to what's already a very digital experience.

You’ve refreshed and updated the rewards proposition for a number of physical card partnerships this year. Is it harder or easier to update a wallet-based product than a traditional card?

It’s different. Samsung owns the experience because it’s sitting inside their wallet. There are a lot of capabilities we have for our other clients that we can make available to them, but the key difference is we have to work with Samsung’s development teams to ensure that we're exposing that – they're making sure this fits the Samsung experience that they're trying to create for their consumers. It creates a new layer of coordination.

As their operating system updates, we can bring things to life in a very seamless way to the consumer. So it’s almost a surprise when they have new features and functionality. But it does require a new layer of coordination, because it's something we're exposing to their property.

What are the next improvements or milestones you're working toward?

I firmly believe that if you have a product that sits in a wallet on your phone, you would want to be able to do everything you can from that. If you want to interact with us through a chat, you should be able to do most things through a chat. Think of every permutation of servicing over time – we would want to be able to do that.

What we launched was the most important things you could do: redeem rewards, do your transactions, pay your bill, lock your card, activate your card. But it’s not exhaustive. There are still things we want to enhance related to the servicing and the usage experience, as well as offering potentially other products in an integrated way. 

Your Frontier partnership isn’t the only long-term one. The co-branded card with Barnes & Noble is about 20 years old, and your partnership with JetBlue is 10. What makes a good refresh of a longstanding partnership?

It used to be that card co-brand card programs might refresh every five or 10 years. What we found is that you need to refresh products more often than that – in many cases, every three or four years. Sometimes the look and the feel of the product just needs to be modernized, but often it's the value proposition that may need to be refreshed. In some cases, consumers want a different product to meet them where they are.

For example, most co-brand products used to offer 1% to 3% in some kind of rewards currency. But now a lot of programs might offer you status; they might offer you lounge access. The consumer may want streaming credits, or they might want quadruple points at grocery stores. You have to adjust your product to meet what the consumer is looking for today, and that could be different than what they were looking for three or five years ago.

title: Bottomline Sees Expertise Turning AI Potential Into Customer Value
snippet: Customers are willing to adopt AI, but they still want guidance from people who understand business, Bottomline SVP, Product Management Jeff Feuerstein writes in a new PYMNTS eBook, “Payments Leaders Rethink What Works in 2026.” In January, I was convinced like many others that we were heading toward a “SaaSpocalypse.” Every week brought another […] The post Bottomline Sees Expertise Turning AI Potential Into Customer Value appeared first on PYMNTS.com.
fullText:
Customers are willing to adopt AI, but they still want guidance from people who understand business, Bottomline SVP, Product Management Jeff Feuerstein writes in a new PYMNTS eBook, “Payments Leaders Rethink What Works in 2026.”

In January, I was convinced like many others that we were heading toward a “SaaSpocalypse.”

Every week brought another headline about artificial intelligence outright replacing software, eliminating the need for specialized applications, and reducing barriers to entry. The prevailing view was, and for some people still is, that AI would become the product, and that years of accumulated expertise embedded in software platforms would become less important.

I wasn’t sure every prediction in that vein would come true, but signs indicated that businesses were searching for technology to solve business problems, and that AI models would become the primary source of competitive advantage.

Over the course of the year, I changed my mind.

It wasn’t because of a single event. Instead, it was a series of conversations with customers and prospects who I expected to be focused on AI as its utility and popularity grew. I kept hearing something different. Customers weren’t asking who had the newest model or the most AI features. They wanted to know who understood their business the best, and then how AI could improve specific issues they were facing.

I saw this repeatedly in payments and financial operations. Customers were willing to adopt AI, but they still wanted guidance from people who understood the sensitivity of payment data, complex payment workflows, fraud risks, compliance requirements, vendor dynamics and the realities of managing payment and financial operations across large teams, organizations and systems. The technology mattered, yes, but expertise was essential to get these customers to trust the solutions.

Customers understood that AI could be disruptive in a good way, but they were not eager to rush to implement it. They wanted to understand how it would impact their existing workflows and what they could reasonably automate with AI. They wanted to know what risks existed and how they could be mitigated with good governance and safeguards. And they wanted to know, above all, how the partners they trusted were using this technology to make finance faster, safer and easier.

That was the insight I hadn’t fully appreciated in January.

Artificial intelligence lowers the cost of creating technology, but it doesn’t eliminate the need for knowledge, experience or trust. Its great speed and promise, paired with its inability to think critically, makes those factors more valuable. As the technology becomes more accessible, expertise becomes a greater differentiator, not a lesser one. The winning combination is knowing how to use AI responsibly, safeguard customers’ data and payments and bring it all together with best-in-class technology.

As a result, I’ve changed how I think about AI heading into this winter. I no longer believe success comes from having the most cutting-edge technology alone. I believe it comes from combining great technology with deep domain expertise and trusted relationships. We are investing in AI because of its transformational promise, but we’re equally focused on the people, partnerships and industry knowledge that help customers turn new technology into business outcomes that matter.

In January, I thought AI would diminish the value of domain expertise because of the universe of possibilities it opened. Today, after seeing where AI is going and hearing from customers who are looking for us to guide the way for them, I believe the opposite. The winners in the AI era will be the companies that combine advanced technology with deep expertise, responsible innovation and the trust to deliver meaningful customer outcomes.

title: Shift4 signals caution
snippet: The payments processor is navigating weak demand for travel to Europe, and softer sales at its restaurant and hotel customers.
fullText:
Troubling economic conditions are continuing to vex Shift4 Payments, with the point-of-sale processor beset by travel weakness in Europe and reduced dining in the U.S.

Shift4 is navigating “a more challenging backdrop than we’ve seen in recent years,” CEO Taylor Lauber wrote in a shareholder letter accompanying the company’s third-quarter results on Thursday. The company cut its profit outlook and gross revenue target for the full year, with weak conditions expected to persist into 2027.

“Our business has been tested in many different ways this year, forcing us to adapt the business and make challenging calls,” Lauber said Thursday on a conference call with analysts to discuss the results. 

Fallout from the Iran conflict has bedeviled Shift4 in the European retail market, where it operates with Global Blue, the Swiss payments technology firm it acquired last year for $2.5 billion, including taking on $1 billion in debt. The Middle East and southeast Asia are significant sources of travel customers for Global Blue’s tax-free shopping business, which represents about 20% of Shift4 revenues. 

Beyond the European retail woes, inflation-fatigued Americans are also dining out less. Restaurant sales not only haven’t improved in the second half of 2026, as the company had expected, some comparisons turned negative in October relative to last year, Chief Financial Officer Christopher Cruz said.

Given the conditions, Shift4 has adopted “a conservatism in the way we're looking at the variety of challenges this year” for its financial modeling, as the overall operating environment makes it “hard not to be influenced towards a more cautious approach,” Cruz said in response to an analyst’s question about factors affecting Shift4’s views of 2027.

Shift4 also announced its purchase of Paramount Commerce, a Toronto-based pay-by-bank firm. Terms of the deal, expected to close in the next few weeks, were not disclosed. Paramount enables pay-by-bank deposits and payouts in Canada for companies that include the sports betting sites DraftKings and FanDuel, and Canadian telecommunications firm Telus, Shift4 said in its Thursday third-quarter earnings presentation.

“Bank rails carry the lion’s share of payment volumes in many markets, and account-to-account fits transactions where cards run into limits,” Lauber said on a conference call Thursday with analysts. “This is a kind of normal-course, tuck-in (purchase) that fits right into the Shift4 playbook.”

One issue troubling investors is that Shift4 has failed to articulate a long-term strategy, “especially around Global Blue,” William Blair analyst Andrew Jeffrey wrote last month in a report for the investment firm’s clients. 

The acquisition occurred under former CEO Jared Isaacman, who left the company last year when he was confirmed as administrator of the National Aeronautics and Space Administration.

“Our sense is that investors still don’t have a good sense of why this deal happened, whether it was the former CEO’s passion project or it simply reflected a desire for scale,” Jeffrey wrote Oct. 20. Shift4 has “substantial cross-sell potential” with Global Blue among its smaller and medium sized business customers, but hasn’t yet demonstrated it can monetize a new POS device it rolled out to 15 European countries this year.

In a note Thursday, Jeffrey further suggested that Shift4 has relied on a dated model of buying independent software vendors and small acquirers at attractive prices, replacing legacy software systems, and monetizing the technology. 

“This strategy was successful when Shift4 was much smaller, money was free, the merchant processing industry was less competitive, and Shift4 had a knowledge advantage,” he wrote. “Those circumstances no longer exist, in our opinion.”

Shift4 shares have lost about 36% over the past year, including a 4.5% drop on Thursday.

“The share price has clearly not reflected the durability, diversity, and outright caliber of our business and the optimism we feel inside the company,” the CEO said, noting in his remarks that Shift4’s employees, management and founder own about 42% of the company, which is based near Allentown, Pennsylvania. 

Later in the call, Lauber said that “market sentiment in both our business and the broader sector is one that is not rewarding much and is punishing any misgivings.”

fullText:
We've intervened and Ethica Resolve Limited (Ethica), an FCA authorised firm that services and collects debt on behalf of creditors, has agreed to restrictions. These follow demands it made for people to repay loans, or purported loans, provided as part of disguised remuneration schemes. 

  

            						

Ethica is acting on behalf of West 28th Street Limited (West 28), which bought disguised remuneration loans from a third party. West 28 is not authorised or regulated by the FCA.

Disguised remuneration schemes saw people – often contractors, consultants and agency workers – paid for their work through loans instead of regular salaries. HMRC has published guidance for those affected.

Some of those affected dispute liability for the amounts being claimed and challenge whether the debts can be legally enforced. If they're unenforceable, borrowers cannot be forced to pay the money back or have any of their assets seized against the debt without a specific order.

Under the requirements we’ve agreed, Ethica:

Will write to affected consumers, explaining that they do not have an enforceable obligation to make payment at this stage. (This means they do not need to pay now while regulatory and legal issues relating to the purported loans are resolved.)

Will not make further demands for payment from affected consumers in the current proposed court claim while regulatory and legal issues are resolved.

Additionally, Ethica and West 28 will not ask a court to make a judgment against someone who has not responded to a legal claim. This is known as a ‘default judgment’.  

However, consumers should not ignore any formal court documents they receive on this issue. They should consider seeking independent legal or debt advice before deciding what to do.

Additional protections for vulnerable consumers are being put in place and Ethica will identify affected consumers who may be vulnerable.

It has not yet been decided whether the debts can be enforced, which may be decided by a court.  

The requirements agreed protect consumers from avoidable harm while the relevant regulatory and legal issues are resolved.  

Consumers should not be subject to undue pressure when being contacted about a debt. If you believe you have been subjected to this type of behaviour, you should report it to us.

title: States keep targeting card fee relief
snippet: Despite legal challenges to the Illinois Interchange Fee Prohibition Act, more than 30 interchange relief bills have been introduced in statehouses this year.
fullText:
As opponents in the legal battle over the Interchange Fee Prohibition Act prepare their motions for the Seventh Circuit U.S. Court of Appeals, legislators in several other states continue to push bills to regulate the card fees.

Bills the payments industry is following closely have been introduced in Pennsylvania, Massachusetts and New Jersey. Each of the three bills seeks to exempt merchants, like retailers and restaurants, from being charged interchange fees on sales tax, and two of them include an interchange exemption for gratuities. 

“I had a liquor store owner tell me that by paying interchange on sales tax, he is getting hit with a fee for collecting sales tax for the state,” New York Assemblyman John T. McDonald III said in an interview last month. McDonald introduced an interchange-relief bill last year and was re-elected to his seat in last week’s election. “Paying interchange on money the state requires merchants to collect on its behalf is unfair,” he said.

What’s drawing attention to the bills in Pennsylvania, Massachusetts and New Jersey is that they could pass before any of the three legislatures adjourns in late 2026 or in early January 2027, not long before oral arguments for the IFPA will be heard late next January by the Seventh Circuit appellate court in Chicago.

“Passing an interchange law before the appeals process in the Seventh Circuit court is settled creates an issue for legislators in other states, because the legal challenge to the IFPA has set a precedent,” Scott Talbott, executive vice president for the Electronic Transactions Association, said last month in an interview. “Pass an interchange-related bill in another state before the legal challenge to the IFPA is settled and a lawsuit is likely to follow.”

In 2026, 32 interchange-related bills were introduced in 20 states, Washington, D.C. and Puerto Rico, according to the ETA. Since 2025, 75 interchange-related bills have been introduced across 32 states, Washington, D.C. and Puerto Rico.

Banks that issue credit cards impose interchange fees on merchants for processing a payment when consumers swipe their credit cards. Those fees are typically separate from other fees charged by the dominant U.S. card networks, Visa and Mastercard, or other intermediaries. Nonetheless, interchange fees often are an inexact reference for all the fees.

Most of the interchange-related bills introduced are focused on exempting sales and tips from the calculation of interchange fees on credit card transactions. 

In New Jersey, for example, Senate bill 4360 prohibits card networks from charging interchange on sales tax or gratuities, “provided the merchant transmits the tax or gratuity amount as part of the authorization or settlement process for the electronic payment transaction.” 

The Senate bill also prohibits card networks from increasing interchange rates on the non-sales tax and gratuity portion of the transaction to compensate for the loss of interchange revenue on tax and gratuities. The bill is currently before the Senate Commerce Committee. 

A companion bill, Assembly bill 5014, has been introduced and referred to the Financial Institutions and Insurance Committee. The New Jersey State Legislature is scheduled to adjourn Dec. 17.

In Massachusetts, Senate bill 688 would also prohibit charging interchange fees on sales tax and gratuities. The bill would make it “unlawful” for issuers, card networks, acquirers or processors from increasing interchange rates to make up for lost interchange revenue on tax or tips. The bill was designated for further study in July. Results of the study are expected before the end of the year. Final adjournment for the Massachusetts legislature’s 2025-2026 session is Jan. 5, 2027. No companion bill was introduced in the House.

In the Pennsylvania House of Representatives, House bill 2090 seeks to prohibit interchange from being charged on sales tax and prohibits card networks from “increasing other fees to circumvent this rule, charging consumers or merchants for disputed transactions before a resolution, or penalizing merchants for setting prices in compliance with the law.”

The bill also requires that card networks “deduct sales tax from interchange fee calculations or provide merchants a rebate for interchange levied on sales tax.” The bill, introduced during the Pennsylvania legislature’s 2025-2026 regular session, has been referred to to the House Finance Committee. The legislature is scheduled to adjourn Nov. 30.

A companion bill, Senate bill 1202 has been introduced in the Pennsylvania Senate and is before the Senate Finance Committee.

All three bills call for the imposition of monetary penalties for parties collecting interchange on sales tax or gratuities.

One driver behind the flurry of bills to regulate interchange at the state level is that sponsors of the bills consider subjecting sales tax, which merchants typically collect on behalf of the state, unreasonable because merchants do not keep that revenue. Sponsors also make the same argument for collecting interchange on tips.

McDonald’s bill, which was introduced in 2025, seeks to prohibit interchange from being levied on sales tax and gratuities. The bill was in committee when the New York Assembly adjourned in June.

The impetus to introduce the bill grew out of McDonald’s experience as a pharmacy owner and pharmacist by profession, and with the national attention the IFPA is attracting. “Cash is no longer king, credit is – we don’t see a lot of cash at my business,” McDonald said.

While McDonald acknowledged that New York pays merchants to collect sales tax, he added the amount is typically not enough to cover the cost of interchange levied on sales tax.

If interchange on tax and gratuities amounted to a few hundred dollars a month, McDonald contends businesses “could live with the cost,” but when interchange fees on tax and tips total $1,000 a month or more, it’s a cost that businesses, especially small businesses, can’t afford to ignore. 

“Affordability has been an ongoing conversation with merchants for years,” said McDonald. “My aim is to try and do something to lower this cost. It’s not just small businesses that are affected, large businesses are affected too. “Most people don’t know the cost impact of interchange on businesses,” he contended.

Like many state legislators, McDonald is paying close attention to the legal challenge to the IFPA. 

In June, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency issued an order declaring that the National Bank Act preempts Illinois from regulating interchange for national banks and federal savings associations. Afterward, U.S. District Judge Virgina Kendall, in the Northern District of Illinois, issued a permanent injunction exempting national banks and federal savings associations from the IFPA, but that doesn’t affect state-charted banks or financial institutions.

Plaintiffs in the case, led by the Illinois Bankers Association, have appealed Kendall’s ruling in an effort to exempt state-charted banks and financial institutions from the IFPA. Plaintiffs have until Dec. 21 to file their brief for the appeal.

“We are looking at every legal avenue to provide relief [from the IFPA] to the entire banking industry,” Carolyn Settanni, executive vice president and general counsel for the Illinois Bankers Association, said last month in an interview. “If one player is left out, it will impact the entire global payments system.”

In the meantime, Illinois Attorney General Kwame Raoul’s office filed notice of an appeal in October requesting the appellate court overturn the lower federal court ruling that national banks and federal savings associations be exempt from the IFPA and that the law be allowed to stand as passed. The Illinois Attorney General has until Nov. 23 to file its brief and until Jan. 11, 2027, to file a reply to the plaintiff’s brief. Oral arguments for the appeals have been set for Jan. 27, 2027.

If plaintiffs in the case succeed in getting the IFPA struck down by the courts, their next step would be to push for the IFPA to be repealed. “It makes no sense to keep a law on the books that is unapplicable,” Ashley Sharp, the Illinois Credit Union League’s chief legal officer and senior vice president of state advocacy, said in an interview last month.

Illinois legislators voted to push the implementation date for the IFPA back to July 1, 2027, to allow time for legal challenges to the law to play out.

While Sharp acknowledges that operating costs for businesses drive a lot of conversation around interchange relief, she argues the IFPA is not the fix merchants need to combat rising operating costs. “Sales costs are rising,” Sharp said. “The broader question is what are all the factors contributing to rising costs for merchants.”

Sharp argues that merchants have pushed to exempt sales taxes and tips from interchange because they do not keep that revenue, but “requiring financial institutions to process these portions of card transactions for free shifts costs rather than eliminating them.”

Interchange also helps fund “a secure payment infrastructure, fraud prevention, and consumer protections that make electronic payments possible,” Sharp added.

If the IFPA is eventually struck down by the courts, legislators in other states are expected to continue introducing bills to provide merchants interchange relief. 

“Merchants are constantly talking to state legislators about affordability and efforts to reduce interchange will continue,” Doug Kantor, general counsel for the National Association of Convenience Stores, said in an interview last month. “There will likely be bills written that avoid, or sidestep, problems the court finds with the IFPA.”

One potential strategy for upholding the IFPA and similar interchange relief bills would be for merchants to challenge the OCC’s ruling that federal banking laws supersede state law. “The OCC’s ruling could be challenged in court,” Kantor said “I don’t see it holding up to scrutiny.”

Should the IFPA be enacted in its current form, Illinois legislators are likely to find themselves facing a conundrum: do they keep the law in place and put state-chartered banks and financial institutions at a financial disadvantage relative to national banks because they can’t collect interchange on tax and tips or do they revise the law. They could also take an entirely different approach to interchange relief.

“What the IFPA does in its current form is punish state-charted banks and financial institutions,” said John Berlau, a senior fellow and director of finance policy at the Competitive Enterprise Institute. 

That anti-regulatory organization opposes the IFPA, as well as interchange relief bills in other states. “The legal challenges to the IFPA should give Illinois legislators, and legislators in other states, pause,” Berlau said in an October interview.

The UK's most innovative businesses often start small.

Before they can develop new technologies, win contracts or expand into new markets, they need access to banking services to help them operate, invest and grow.

Access to financial services can be easy to take for granted. When those services work well they're almost invisible. However, when access becomes difficult or delayed, the effects can extend far beyond a single business.

Small-to-medium sized enterprises (SMEs) operating in or providing services to the defence sector play an important role in innovation and growth.

But these businesses do more than contribute to economic growth. Many are helping to develop the technologies, expertise and capabilities that support the UK's national resilience and security.

Banking services are part of that story. They help businesses secure contracts, invest in new opportunities and grow. They are one of the key links between innovation and capability, and between economic growth and national resilience.

That's why we wanted to understand whether defence SMEs were able to access banking services efficiently and consistently.

The challenge for defence SMEs is friction and delay, not exclusion

The current debate around defence and financial services has, at times, suggested that defence businesses are routinely excluded from accessing financial services. But for everyday banking services, such as opening a bank account, the picture is a lot more nuanced.

The firms we engaged with can and do serve defence SMEs. Many are taking steps to better understand and support the sector. In some cases, they're investing in specialist expertise, dedicated teams and governance processes.

But we also heard about long onboarding processes, repeated requests for information and delays in decision-making.

The theme that emerged was friction and delay rather than widespread exclusion.

That distinction matters because it points to a different challenge. The question is not whether firms are willing to serve the sector, but whether their processes are proportionate to the risks. And whether firms can reduce friction while managing risk effectively. SMEs can also help by being prepared to explain how they manage the risks associated with their business, and by providing clear and timely information to firms.

Defence is not one-size-fits-all

There is no regulatory barrier preventing firms from supporting lawful defence businesses. Financial services firms are entitled to make commercial decisions and determine their own risk appetite. But the approach they take should be proportionate to the specific risks.

One of the strongest messages from our work is that defence should not be viewed as a single category.

The sector is vast. It includes businesses that directly support the UK's defence capabilities, as well as those that are linked through the products, services or technologies they provide including software, logistics, maintenance, engineering, manufacturing and consulting. Their activities, business models and risk profiles can differ significantly.

Whatever the business model, robust due diligence to manage financial crime and other risks remains essential. But effective risk management is also about recognising differences.

A risk-based approach should focus on the specific customer, the activities they undertake and the risks they present.

Better information leads to better decisions

Another theme that stood out was the importance of data.

Many firms told us they do not always have a clear picture of their defence customers or the outcomes those customers experience throughout their journey with the firm.

Without good information, it becomes harder for firms to answer important questions including:

Are applications taking longer than expected?

Are decisions being applied consistently?

Do governance processes reflect actual risk?

Are customers receiving outcomes that align with the firm's stated approach?

Good management information helps firms answer those questions. It supports stronger oversight, better decision-making and ultimately better customer outcomes.

Getting the balance right

Our work does not introduce new rules or requirements. But it does reinforce an important principle: firms should take risk-based and proportionate decisions based on the circumstances of individual customers, including SMEs.

When firms get that balance right, they can manage risk effectively while helping viable businesses access the services they need to invest, innovate and grow.

Ultimately, we hope this work helps firms strike that balance and ensures that businesses contributing to the UK's national resilience can access the banking services they need to succeed.

title: Brits nearly twice as likely to spot pressure tactics in horror films as investment red flags

A survey of UK 18 to 40-year-olds who own or are considering investments found 65% spotted ‘this is your only chance’ as a classic horror warning sign. But when faced with a ‘last chance to buy’ investment opportunity, only 36% said it would make them more cautious, while 37% said they would feel pressure to buy quickly or risk missing out. Investors are almost twice as likely to recognise pressure tactics in a horror film as they are when those tactics are used to promote an investment opportunity, new FCA data suggests.

  

            						

A survey of UK 18 to 40-year-olds who own or are considering investments found 65% spotted ‘this is your only chance’ as a classic horror warning sign. But when faced with a ‘last chance to buy’ investment opportunity, only 36% said it would make them more cautious, while 37% said they would feel pressure to buy quickly or risk missing out.  

The pattern also holds for other pressure tactics. While 59% recognised countdowns like the ticking clock in 'Saw' as a tactic designed to make characters act rashly, just 5% said they would be suspicious of the pressure created by a rising investment price graph.

Yet only 12% were similarly sceptical of a 'groundbreaking new' investment product, while 1 in 10 said being new would actually make them more likely to invest.  

Peer pressure and hype also influenced attitudes towards investment. While 80% recognised ‘trust me, it's fine, everyone's doing it’ as a warning sign in a horror scenario, almost 3 in 10 (29%) said excitement from friends or group chats about an investment would reassure them or make them trust the opportunity rather than doing their own research.  

Lucy Castledine, director of consumer investments at the FCA, said: 'Many people can spot a horror movie trap a mile off, but this survey suggests they’re far less likely to recognise the same tactics when they're used to influence investment decisions. The FCA's InvestSmart campaign helps consumers make more informed investment decisions. Its Hype Type Revealer helps people understand what may influence their decisions and how to avoid being drawn in by investment hype.

Research conducted by Attest on behalf of the FCA. Fieldwork conducted on 9 October 2026. Around half of respondents hold a stocks and shares ISA.

Demands for disguised remuneration scheme loan repayments

              

  

  

  
    

        

    

      

We have seen demands being made for people to repay loans, or purported loans, provided as part of disguised remuneration schemes.

  

            						

Disguised remuneration schemes saw people – often contractors, consultants and agency workers – paid for their work through loans instead of regular salaries as a way to avoid tax. HMRC has sought to tackle this tax avoidance through what has been termed the loan charge and published guidance for those affected.

Questions have been raised about the regulatory status of these loans and whether they were ever intended to be repaid.

Some of those affected dispute liability for the amounts being claimed and challenge whether the debts can be legally enforced. If they’re unenforceable, borrowers cannot be forced to pay the money back or have any of their assets seized against the debt without a specific order.

Some consumers are, however being sent legal letters threatening potential court action and asking for immediate repayment of the loan. Repayment is being sought after these disguised remuneration loans were sold by the original provider to a third party.

Those seeking payment may ask the FCA to agree to a Validation Order. This is the formal permission needed before the loans could be enforced. We would consider any request carefully and our agreement is by no means guaranteed. If a Validation Order is required and not granted, the debt would remain unenforceable.

Anyone who receives a demand for repayment of a disguised remuneration loan, and is unsure whether they are liable for the amount claimed, should consider carefully whether to make any payment. We’d encourage them to look at the HMRC guidance and consider taking legal advice.

Consumers should not be subject to undue pressure when being contacted about a debt. If you believe you have been subjected to this type of behaviour, you should report it to us.

If you are experiencing any difficulties, whether they are health, money or other difficulties, or if you don't understand what is happening, you should raise this with those contacting you.

Growing companies are finding that stronger sales don’t automatically bring a clearer view of cash, and their finance chiefs are directing investment toward closing that gap.

The PYMNTS Intelligence report “Growth and Scaling: The Corporate Finance Inflection Point,” published in August, was based on a June survey of 60 chief financial officers at companies in the United States generating $100 million to $1 billion annually. It found that even though 58% of firms increased revenue over the prior 24 months, 62% reported difficulty managing or scaling cash flow forecasting. The encouraging finding was that executives have identified practical improvements that can help them see their cash position more clearly and prepare for further growth.

Key findings from the report:

Cash visibility presents the biggest financial challenge. Cash flow forecasting was the single most difficult finance or back-office task for 37% of firms. Looking more broadly, the 62% reporting forecasting difficulties exceeded the share struggling with reconciliation, or matching financial records, by 20 percentage points. A forecast works like a windshield. Finance leaders need a clear view of what’s ahead to decide when they can spend and when they should conserve cash. Disconnected information makes that view harder to maintain.

Operational changes put more pressure on the information behind forecasts. Among firms making at least three significant business changes, 59% reported difficulty bringing data together, compared with 24% of firms making fewer changes. Reconciliation difficulties followed a similar pattern, at 59% versus 27%. These gaps showed why cash visibility depends on work across the finance department. Adding customers or products creates more information to collect and check, even before a company sees the full revenue benefit.

CFOs are targeting investments that address these weaknesses. Cash flow forecasting led their investment priorities at 52%, followed by real-time reporting at 35%. Another 33% prioritized reducing manual processes and 32% aimed to unify finance data. These choices suggested executives want a more dependable view of money coming in and going out. The report also found that automation and data integration helped firms manage complexity across different levels of uncertainty and operational change.

Other findings reinforced the opportunity to improve before growth creates further strain. The report revealed that 62% of CFOs said their finance and back-office systems were at least mostly prepared for the next 24 months, although only 12% reported complete readiness. Standardizing processes received the strongest positive assessment among approaches to managing complexity, followed by automation and data integration.

For firms planning their next expansion, the results offer the practical starting point of making financial information easier to assemble and use.

Kickstarter is connecting crowdfunding campaigns more directly to eCommerce fulfillment, launching an official app in the Shopify App Store that lets creators transfer finalized backer orders into their Shopify stores.

Available Wednesday (Nov. 11), the integration connects Kickstarter’s Pledge Manager, its post-campaign tool for collecting shipping information, taxes and add-on purchases, with Shopify’s commerce platform. Creators can sync finalized orders to Shopify for fulfillment and automatically send tracking information back to Kickstarter, where backers can follow their shipments.

The integration is designed for creators who use Kickstarter to introduce products and build initial demand but rely on Shopify to manage ongoing sales and fulfillment. It eliminates the need to export and reformat spreadsheets before uploading backer orders into Shopify.

The app allows creators to match Kickstarter reward variants with Shopify products using stock keeping unit (SKU) numbers. They can transfer orders in batches, pause or resume synchronization and schedule multiple waves of fulfillment. Backers have 48 hours to confirm their shipping addresses before orders are transferred.

The launch reflects the growing overlap between crowdfunding and traditional online retail. Platforms such as Kickstarter can help businesses validate demand and finance initial production, while commerce infrastructure gives successful campaigns a way to manage fulfillment and subsequent sales through established retail operations.

For creators, that distinction becomes more important as campaigns generate larger order volumes. Kickstarter’s integration is intended to make the transition from a funded project to a functioning commerce operation less dependent on manual processes. Its Pledge Manager also integrates with ShipStation.

The app is free for Kickstarter creators using Pledge Manager, although standard Kickstarter crowdfunding fees still apply. Users need a launched Pledge Manager, Shopify administrator access and matching SKUs for their products and Kickstarter rewards.

“Kickstarter is where creators prove there’s demand for an idea, and Shopify is where they grow it into a business,” Jeff Kennedy, who works in partnerships at Shopify, said in a statement.

              Highlights            
          

          

                                  

                    

                        In September, 41% of U.S. adults lived paycheck to paycheck and kept up with bills, compared with 25% who lived paycheck to paycheck and struggled to pay them.                      

                  

                                  

                    

                        Among buyers who considered subscriptions optional, the share who would cut them early was 18 percentage points higher for consumers living paycheck to paycheck and keeping up with bills.

Consumers who lived paycheck to paycheck and kept up with their bills bought from an average of 1.9 discretionary categories over the previous year. That put them closer to consumers who struggled to pay bills, who bought from 1.6 categories, than to those who didn’t live paycheck to paycheck, who bought from 2.5.

The two groups farthest apart in what they bought were closer in what they considered optional, as PYMNTS Intelligence found. Consumers who kept up with bills while living paycheck to paycheck classified an average of 10.5 of 22 categories as discretionary, compared with 10.1 among those who didn’t live paycheck to paycheck. In the September survey of 2,487 U.S. adults, counted a purchase as discretionary only when the respondent considered the category optional.

Among people who made discretionary purchases, 40% of those living paycheck to paycheck without difficulty paying bills rated at least one category a notable or major expense in a typical month. The share was also 40% among buyers who struggled to pay bills, compared with 34% among buyers who didn’t live paycheck to paycheck. The annual count measures how widely consumers bought across categories. The monthly rating captures how much those purchases mattered to buyers’ budgets.

Where Buyers Would Cut

Subscriptions show how differently buyers with similar views of what’s optional would respond if money got tighter. Among consumers who bought subscriptions and considered them discretionary, 57% of those living paycheck to paycheck and keeping up with bills would put them among their first cuts. That was three percentage points below the share among buyers struggling to pay bills and 18 points above the share among those who didn’t live paycheck to paycheck.

When consumers picked a discretionary expense to cut first, their reasons varied little across financial groups. In each group, 49% to 54% said the purchase was something they wanted more than something they needed. Another frequently cited reason was that the expense was easy to stop, at 43% to 44%.

At the other end of the budget, about 27% of consumers who kept up with bills while living paycheck to paycheck named mortgage or homeownership costs as the expense they would protect longest. The share was about the same among consumers who didn’t live paycheck to paycheck. For these two groups, the top priority was the same even though their willingness to cut subscriptions differed by 18 points.

fullText:
How many of us read the terms and conditions of a contract before buying a financial product?

Contracts hold the detail that shapes everyone's financial life, whether you're taking out a loan, insuring your holiday, or signing up for a crypto wallet.

All firms are responsible for making sure that terms in their consumer contracts comply with the fairness and transparency requirements of the Consumer Rights Act (CRA) 2015. When those terms don’t comply, our Consumer Contracts team has powers to challenge firms directly.

This work shows how we use the full range of powers Parliament has given us, not only those in financial services legislation, to tackle harm.

Here's why it matters: if a term is found to be unfair, it's not just unenforceable – consumers may be due redress too. That's why it pays for firms to get this right from the start.

We review contract terms identified through our supervision of firms, information on social media, and referrals from consumers and other external stakeholders.  

When we take action  

We consider our rules and guidance, including the Consumer Duty, when deciding whether to act and which of our regulatory tools to use.  

Where we raise concerns about the fairness or transparency of terms, we expect firms to:  

Amend or delete the relevant terms so that the contract is fair and transparent, and stop relying on those terms in existing contracts.

Pay redress to consumers if the firm’s use of the terms has caused harm; and

In some cases, give us a voluntary undertaking under the CRA.  

Where necessary, we can apply for a court injunction to prevent a firm from using or enforcing the term against its customers. We can also seek a court order requiring it to pay redress.  

Examples of cases we've tackled

A crypto firm agreed to stop charging excessive storage fees which, in some cases, could exceed £40,000 a year. We intervened after finding it had charged inactive customers a disproportionate amount. The firm removed the term and paid redress to affected consumers.

A financial adviser updated its contracts after trying to charge a customer £800 for time spent handling a complaint. The charge was included in its terms and conditions, but we considered the term unfair because it could put people off making legitimate complaints. We also considered it inconsistent with the Consumer Duty and our own rules.

A travel insurer clarified unclear terms about what counted as a 12-hour delay and paid out £18,000 in redress to customers whose claims had been wrongly denied. Here, ambiguous wording was the problem, so we pushed for clearer terms that told consumers exactly what they were entitled to.

A lender improved the terms of a new credit product to give clearer information on costs and cancellation rights after we raised concerns ahead of launch. This is a good example of intervening early, through the authorisations process, to prevent unfair terms making it to market in the first place.

What we expect of firms

Firms should regularly check that their consumer contracts are fair, clear and transparent, and that they're being used fairly in practice.  

In practice, that means:

Taking into account consumers’ legitimate interests when designing contracts.

Using plain language, so customers understand what they're agreeing to: for example, what they might have to pay and what rights they have. Nobody should need a law degree to understand what they're signing up to.  

Avoiding surprises, by making important terms – fees, cancellation rights, variations, exclusions, complaints – easy to spot.

Reviewing contracts regularly to stay compliant with the latest requirements, rulings and judgments, and to learn from complaints, claims, cancellations, fees, customer outcomes and other data.

Testing whether customers actually understand key terms – not just assuming they do.

Improving staff training to ensure staff meet the standards set out in product literature, including contracts. Using complaints data to identify potentially unfair or unclear contract terms and make appropriate changes.

How to report concerns about unfair or unclear terms to us

Concerned about an unfair or unclear term in a financial services firm’s consumer contract? You can report it to us using our form. We can't always tell you what action we've taken, but, we can assure you, every report we receive gets considered.

title: Block to provide data to FTC
snippet: The company said it will turn over documents the Federal Trade Commission sought in January in response to a probe of complaints about Square.
fullText:
An article from

The company said it will turn over documents the Federal Trade Commission sought in January in response to a probe of complaints about Square.

        

            

        Published Nov. 10, 2026
    

                        

                            

                                
                            

                

                

    
        

        

    
            
                The Federal Trade Commission offices on Pennsylvania Avenue in Washington DC.
            
        
            Getty Images
        
    
    
    

Dive Brief:

Block will comply with a Federal Trade Commission request for information as part of a regulatory inquiry into some 1,500 merchant complaints alleging the company froze or deactivated Square user accounts without notice. Block said in a court filing Friday that it would produce the materials the agency sought in three batches by year-end.

“For the sake of efficiency and to avoid the burden and delay of litigation, the parties now wish to resolve the issues in the Petition, and all other issues related to compliance with” the FTC’s civil investigative demand, attorneys for Block and the FTC said in a joint filing to the federal court. Block said it “disputes and does not admit the allegations” in the agency’s petition.

The FTC argued in a court filing last month that Block had not complied with its Jan. 22 civil investigative demand, despite several meetings between attorneys for the parties. The agency asked U.S. Magistrate Judge Sallie Kim to enforce its investigative demand.

Dive Insight:

Besides the Square point-of-sale business, Block owns Cash App and Afterpay, a buy now, pay later service. The Oakland, California-based company was founded and is led by Jack Dorsey, who also founded the social media company Twitter.

The Square user complaints at issue “allege that Block has wrongfully withheld at least $2.5 million of Square users’ payment proceeds since 2022,” the FTC said in its Oct. 7 filing with the U.S. District Court in San Francisco. “Given the FTC’s experience that only a small fraction of injured consumers complain to the government, these losses may be just the tip of the iceberg,” the regulator said.

Spokespeople for the FTC and Block declined to comment Monday on the filing or about which time period the alleged Square complaints cover.

Block agreed to respond to 47 interrogatories the FTC has posed about the Square matter and produce all non-privileged documents and non-privileged portions of partially privileged documents by Nov. 13, according to the joint filing. Block also will make a second submission to the FTC of additional information by Nov. 30. By year-end, Block also will turn over “all responsive non-privileged documents with one or more search term hits” detailed in an email last month between the parties, the filing said.

The request contained 47 questions, 21 documents requests and four separate data requests, according to the FTC’s October filing for the court’s intervention.

The FTC’s attorneys said its January demand gave Block until Feb. 18 to seek to quash or modify the agency’s request, “but Block never filed a petition to quash or modify the CID (demand), nor sought any extension of time to file the petition.”

Block’s attorneys with Gibson Dunn & Crutcher also asked the court Friday to seal some “confidential information that would cause Block particularized business harm if it were disclosed publicly.” The request pertains to Block presentations to directors and senior executives about its fraud-prevention and risk-management efforts, the company said.

The investigative demand is the third by a government agency against Block since 2021, the FTC noted in its petition to the court, citing court requests by the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau and the Washington state attorney general.
