title: California takes CoinFlip to task
snippet: The state ordered the crypto ATM company to pay $4.8 million to scam victims, and bashed federal regulators over failing to police for fraud.
fullText:
California regulators demanded this week that crypto ATM operator CoinFlip pay scam victims $4.8 million in restitution for fraud that took place at the company’s machines in the state.

The state’s new Business and Consumer Services Agency, tasked with protecting consumers from financial fraud, issued a notice Thursday saying CoinFlip had violated state and federal laws by not better protecting its customers from fraud that was perpetrated through the company’s machines that exchange cash for crypto.

“An investigation by California's Department of Financial Protection and Innovation found that, over the past five years, CoinFlip failed to detect, prevent, report, and mitigate suspicious activity, paving the way for scammers to exploit Californians and steal their hard–earned money,” the California agency said in the release.

The regulators noted that some of the laws that were breached by CoinFlip are expressly to protect Californians using crypto kiosks.

CoinFlip didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

CoinFlip, which is based in Chicago and was founded in 2015, says on its website that it is the world’s “largest network of cryptocurrency ATMs by transaction volume.” It offers services at some 5,500 bitcoin ATMs in six countries, including 48 states in the U.S., according to the website. About 500 of the company’s crypto kiosks exist in California, typically at grocery and convenience stores or gas stations, according to the state agency. 

Crypto fraud is an expanding part of schemes that target the elderly, including in scams where criminals lure consumers to provide funds under false pretenses, sometimes asking them to transfer money.

“Because transactions are immediate, hard to track, and cannot be reversed, crypto ATMs like those in CoinFlip's network have become the tool of choice for fraudsters looking to exploit consumers — especially older Americans,” the California release said.

California’s Business and Consumer Services Agency was conceived last year as part of a restructuring of state agencies by Gov. Gavin Newsom, a Democrat. The revised government structure was finalized in July of this year.

The action against CoinFlip “is the latest example of our work to ensure new technology actually helps people, rather than driving up prices or opening the doors to fraud — a key priority of California's consumer watchdog agency,” the release said.

Rohit Chopra was appointed in May to lead the new California agency. He formerly headed the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau during President Joe Biden’s administration, and left the CFPB post last year after President Donald Trump became president. Chopra also was Commissioner at the Federal Trade Commission until 2021 during Trump’s first administration.

With the start of the second Trump Administration, the CFPB’s workforce was chopped and the president’s leadership expressed an interest in shuttering the agency. The agency has since reversed course on policies that were put in place by Chopra, including with respect to emerging digital financial service offerings.

Chopra took a swipe at the Trump administration polices in the release announcing the state’s action against CoinFlip. His comments landed in a week in which Democrats broadly won elections nationwide, both at the federal and state levels. Newsom has widely been seen as a potential 2028 presidential candidate.

“As federal regulators give a free pass to crimes against consumers, California continues to chart a different path. While consumers can no longer rely on federal regulators to protect them, we are doubling down to ensure that new technology does not turbocharge fraud and that bad actors are held accountable,” the release said.

title: Merchant Payments Conference MPE to Mark 20th Edition in Berlin
snippet: Merchant Payments Ecosystem (MPE) marks its 20th edition in Berlin in March 2027, with AI, stablecoins and merchant payments on the agenda. The post Merchant Payments Conference MPE to Mark 20th Edition in Berlin appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
When the European Card Acquiring Forum first met in 2008, just 18 merchants were among its 189 delegates. The event, now known as Merchant Payments Ecosystem (MPE), is preparing for its 20th edition, with more than 500 merchants expected to attend in Berlin next March.

Taking place from 9 to 11 March 2027 at the InterContinental Berlin, the conference is expected to attract more than 1,600 payments professionals. Its programme will cover artificial intelligence (AI), agentic commerce, stablecoins, payment orchestration and cross-border payments.

MPE has grown from a conference focused on card acquiring to one covering a much wider range of payments topics. The 2027 event will feature more than 170 speakers and 100 sponsors and partners.

“Twenty years ago, we started MPE with a simple idea: put the people shaping European merchant payments in one room, ask the questions that matter, and give them a platform to exchange ideas,” said Natalia Ivanis, co-founder and chief marketing officer of MPE. 

“That room has grown into a strategic meeting place for senior leaders from merchants and the companies that serve them, but some of the questions never went away. Our 20th edition is about looking back at them and asking where merchant payments go next. The questions changed. The need for clarity didn’t.” 

Marking 20 years

MPE is also publishing a series of articles and interviews about the history of European merchant payments. Its 20 Voices series includes contributions from Omnipay founder Hubert O’Donoghue. Neira Jones, chair of the MPE Awards judging panel, is also putting together a five-chapter history of the industry, which is due to be published in full in January 2027.

O’Donoghue, founder of Omnipay, says: “Over a decade on, the ubiquity of payment channels across almost every facet of human activity, coupled with the arrival of AI, presents new challenges for audit, control, authentication, and verification.”

The MPE 2027 conference will also include the annual MPE Awards, with entries for the 2027 awards opening in November. Early-bird passes are available at 20% off until 11 November, followed by 10% off until 16 December.

title: Will a ‘blue wave’ push the CCCA?
snippet: With Sen. Roger Marshall voted out and Sen. Dick Durbin retiring, the Credit Card Competition Act faces an uncertain future.
fullText:
The ‘blue wave’ of Democrat victories in Congress this week washed Republican Sen. Roger Marshall out of office, tapering his support for the Credit Card Competition Act.

Sen. Dick Durbin, the Democrat who has been his partner in the push to pass that bill aimed at lowering card swipe fees for merchants, has already said he’s retiring at the end of this term.

That means that at the start of a new Congress next year, the bill won’t have its two biggest co-sponsors of the past few years in the Senate. That could make a meaningful difference for a piece of legislation that has struggled to win passage since Durbin and Marshall first introduced the legislation in 2022.

The bill, which takes aim at Visa and Mastercard, would force banks that issue credit cards to ensure that an alternative card network, other than those two dominant players, was available to process a transaction. The idea is to create more competition in the card network market in a bid to lower fees that merchants are charged for processing cards.

CCCA proponent Doug Kantor, who has long worked on behalf of merchants as general counsel for the National Association of Convenience Stores, called it “painful” to lose Marshall’s support of the legislation. 

But Kantor noted in an interview Wednesday that Marshall has helped win more support of the bill in this congressional session, including from President Donald Trump. Kantor counted nine times that Trump or Vice President JD Vance, a former Senate sponsor of the bill, have publicly called for passage of the legislation. Albeit, much of that public promotion came as part of their failed efforts to see Marshall reelected.

Backers of the bill could still seek to advance it in the final two months of this year, before the two-year congressional session ends and the newly elected senators and representatives arrive, but Kantor didn’t seem hopeful. 

He said it depends on how productive the senators and representatives decide to be when they return to Washington. There are still some spending bills that will move this year and they could be vehicles for carrying the bill across the finish line.

The bill has “as good a shot as many other things to move,” offered Kantor, who also sits on the executive committee of the Merchants Payments Coalition.

However, with so many senators and representatives headed for an exit, and a Thanksgiving Day respite from campaigning just a few weeks away, it’s easy to see them coasting toward the year-end break. 

When asked about future support for the bill, a spokesperson for Durbin pointed to Sen. Peter Welch, a Democrat from Vermont who has been a Senate sponsor of the legislation, and was also in his prior role as a House representative. Durbin this month handed the torch to Welch, according to a report from the political publication PunchBowl News.

The bill benefited from having a Republican leaning in alongside a Democrat, with Marshall throwing his weight behind Durbin’s longtime fight against the top credit card networks. The legislation also had bipartisan backing in the House, where Republican Rep. Lance Good of Texas and Democratic Rep. Zoe Lofgren of California have supported the bill. Both hung onto their seats. 

As far as finding a new Senate Republican to champion the bill, Kantor suggested the existing sponsors would fill that need. With Sen. Cynthia Lummis retiring, that would seem to leave only Sen. Bernie Moreno of Ohio, a state that just returned Democrat Sherrod Brown to the chamber in the latest election.

Opponents of the bill have no doubt that the merchant advocates of the legislation will keep up their years-long campaign to pass the bill. The Electronic Payments Coalition is one of the groups that has battled the bill. They’re bracing for the ongoing clash.

“Our work will continue to focus on educating Americans and policymakers about the real-world consequences of proposed credit card legislation, including its potential impact on small business and consumer access to credit, community financial institutions, data security protections, and cash back and other rewards programs,” EPC Executive Chairman Richard Hunt told members of that group in an emailed note Wednesday morning.

Hunt noted CCCA proponents, including at the National Restaurant Association, are casting the legislation as an “affordability” issue, a theme that helped Democrats win seats across the country. Backers of the bill argue that merchants paying higher fees means prices go up for consumers.

If that becomes the central thrust, there’s always the possibility that the new Congress moves right past paying attention to card fees paid by merchants, and focuses instead on interest rates paid by card holding consumers. 

That might play into the hands of Sens. Bernie Sanders, an Independent from Vermont, and Josh Hawley, a Republican from Missouri, who will remain in the next Congress. Last year, they introduced a bill to cap card interest rates at 10% and will presumably keep pushing for passage.

It’s a bill that has also won backing from Trump and might have improved chances with more Democrats on Capitol Hill.
